Segmentation (VLANs, firewalls between segments, microsegmentation) means a compromised machine in the Finance VLAN cannot reach HR or Engineering VLANs. Ransomware worms that spread across networks (like NotPetya) are contained by segmentation boundaries. Application allow listing (B) would prevent ransomware from executing but doesn't address network spread. Decommissioning (C) retires unused systems. Configuration enforcement (D) ensures secure settings. The keyword "only affect one department" = segmentation/containment.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Network segmentation) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company implements a policy where only applications on a pre-approved list are allowed to execute on corporate workstations. Any other application is automatically blocked. What mitigation technique is this?
questions.justification: Application allow listing (formerly whitelisting) is the security control that permits ONLY pre-approved, known-good applications to execute. Default behavior is DENY — everything not explicitly approved is blocked. This is highly effective against malware because even brand-new, never-before-seen malware (including zero-days) cannot execute if it's not on the approved list. The contrast: deny listing (A) blocks known-bad applications and allows everything else — weaker because new malware isn't on the deny list yet. Configuration enforcement (B) ensures secure settings, not application control. Least privilege (D) controls what users CAN do within applications, not which applications can run. "Only pre-approved list can run, everything else blocked" = allow listing.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Application allow listing) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization discovers that an attacker moved laterally from a compromised HR workstation to the production database server because both were on the same network segment. What mitigation would MOST directly prevent this lateral movement?

options.text: Installing endpoint protection on all systems
Network segmentation with access control between segments

questions.justification: The specific problem is lateral movement between systems on the same network segment. The HR workstation should never be able to initiate connections to the production database server. Segmentation places them on different network segments with a firewall/ACL between them — the firewall enforces that HR workstations cannot reach database servers unless explicitly permitted. Patching (A) would prevent the initial compromise but doesn't stop lateral movement once the workstation is compromised. Encrypting the database (B) protects data if the database is breached but doesn't prevent an authenticated attacker from reaching it. Endpoint protection (C) might detect the lateral movement attempt but doesn't architecturally prevent it. Segmentation is the architectural solution that makes lateral movement require crossing a security boundary.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Network segmentation with access control between segments) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security team is hardening all servers. Which action would MOST effectively reduce the attack surface by eliminating unnecessary communication channels that attackers could exploit?

options.text: Disabling unused ports and protocols (Telnet, FTP, SMBv1)

questions.justification: The question specifically asks about "eliminating unnecessary communication channels." Open ports and enabled protocols ARE the communication channels. Disabling Telnet, FTP, SMBv1, and other unneeded protocols directly removes those attack vectors — an attacker cannot exploit a service that isn't running and a port that isn't open. Each open port is a potential entry point. Changing passwords (A) addresses authentication weaknesses but doesn't eliminate communication channels. Host-based firewalls (C) can block traffic to ports, but disabling the service entirely is more secure — a firewall can be misconfigured, but a disabled service can't be reached at all. Removing software (D) addresses applications, not network ports/protocols specifically. "Communication channels" → ports/protocols.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Disabling unused ports and protocols (Telnet, FTP, SMBv1)) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A database administrator has been granted full root access to every system in the organization to "make their job easier." A security auditor flags this as a violation of which security principle?
questions.justification: Least privilege (also called principle of least privilege / PoLP) states that users, processes, and systems should have only the MINIMUM access necessary to perform their specific function. A DBA needs access to databases — not root access to every system. Granting excess access violates least privilege by giving far more permissions than required. The risk: if the DBA account is compromised, the attacker has root access everywhere. Separation of duties (A) prevents one person from having end-to-end control of a critical process (e.g., the person who approves payments shouldn't also make payments). Defense in depth (C) is the strategy of multiple layered security controls. Zero trust (D) is the architecture of "never trust, always verify." The DBA root access issue is clearly least privilege.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Least privilege) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company is retiring a fleet of 200 laptops. The security team must ensure that sensitive customer data on these devices cannot be recovered. What decommissioning step is MOST appropriate for the hard drives?

options.text: Delete all files and format the drives before donation
Move data to cloud storage then wipe drives once
Use DoD-standard data wiping software or physically destroy the drives
Remove the drives from laptops and store in a locked room

questions.justification: Secure decommissioning requires ensuring data CANNOT be recovered. Simple deletion (A) only removes file system pointers — data is still on the disk and easily recoverable with forensic tools. Moving to cloud and single-wipe (B) is insufficient — one pass may not be enough for modern drives and doesn't address cloud security. Storing drives (D) just delays the problem. Proper decommissioning options: (1) Cryptographic erasure — if the drive is encrypted, delete the encryption key (data becomes unreadable). (2) DoD-standard overwriting (multiple passes of random data). (3) Physical destruction — shredding, degaussing, incineration — the most certain method. For drives with highly sensitive data (PII, customer data), physical destruction or certified wiping with verification is the standard.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key C (certified wiping or physical destruction) is correct for asset disposal; 'DoD-standard' multi-pass wording is dated but the answer is sound.

questions.question: SCENARIO: Three months after a disgruntled employee was terminated, the company discovers that all financial records for that quarter have been deleted from the database at exactly midnight on the employee's last day — the trigger being a specific date. What malware type is this, and who is the most likely threat actor?

options.text: Worm — Organized crime for financial gain

questions.justification: This scenario has three clear indicators pointing to one answer: (1) Logic bomb: malware that remains DORMANT until a specific trigger condition is met — in this case, a date/time trigger ("midnight on last day"). The deletion happened automatically based on a pre-set trigger. (2) Insider threat: the malware was planted by someone with legitimate access to the database, clearly before their termination — only an insider could have placed it. (3) Revenge motivation: the employee was disgruntled and terminated — classic revenge motivation for an insider threat. Logic bombs are specifically associated with insider threats as the planting mechanism. The 3-month gap between termination and execution demonstrates the dormancy aspect of a logic bomb perfectly.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Logic bomb — Insider threat (revenge motivation)) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A researcher discovers that a banking application uses a TLS 1.3 connection by default, but an attacker can force the connection to downgrade to TLS 1.1 by manipulating the initial handshake. What is this attack, and what is the BEST mitigation?

options.text: Downgrade attack; disable older TLS versions and enforce minimum TLS 1.2 or 1.3
Birthday attack; use longer hash functions

questions.justification: A downgrade attack forces a system to use a WEAKER protocol version than it supports. By manipulating the TLS handshake to make the server "think" the client only supports TLS 1.1, the attacker gets a connection using a weaker protocol with known exploitable vulnerabilities. The attacker can then exploit weaknesses in TLS 1.1 that don't exist in TLS 1.3. The mitigation: configure the server to refuse connections below TLS 1.2 — if TLS 1.1 is simply not supported, the downgrade is impossible. The attack works because the server is willing to fall back. Remove that willingness. POODLE was a real downgrade attack against SSL 3.0. Many modern security standards (PCI DSS, NIST) mandate TLS 1.2 minimum, with 1.3 preferred.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Downgrade attack; disable older TLS versions and enforce minimum TLS 1.2 or 1.3) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: During a security assessment, a pen tester finds that 35 network cameras at a corporate facility still use the manufacturer's default username "admin" and password "admin." What is the MOST efficient mitigation for this widespread issue?

options.text: Place cameras on a separate network segment
Disable the cameras until credentials are changed
Immediately change all default credentials and implement a configuration management process to enforce this for future deployments
Apply firmware updates to all cameras

questions.justification: The immediate action AND the systemic fix are both required for a complete answer. Immediately changing all 35 default credentials addresses the current vulnerability. Implementing a configuration management process (requiring default credential changes before deployment) prevents this from recurring. Option A (segmentation) is a good additional defense layer but doesn't fix the root cause — attackers on that segment can still access cameras with default creds. Option B (disabling) is too disruptive and temporary. Option D (firmware) is important for vulnerabilities but doesn't address the default credential problem — firmware updates won't change credentials. The two-part answer (fix now + process to prevent recurrence) is the most complete and correct response to a systemic misconfiguration finding.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key C is correct, but it is the only long, two-part option, which makes it guessable by length rather than knowledge.

questions.question: COMPREHENSIVE SCENARIO: A financial services company suffers a breach. Investigation reveals: (1) An employee clicked a targeted email with their name and position included (2) The email contained a link that installed malware when clicked (3) The malware spread across all systems because no network separation existed (4) Attacker accessed financial records for 6 months before detection (5) No logs existed for the critical systems during the attack period.Match each finding to its correct security term:

options.text: (1)Spear phishing, (2)Malware-laden file, (3)Flat network/no segmentation, (4)APT dwell time, (5)Missing logs/log tampering

questions.justification: (1) Spear phishing: The email included the employee's name and position — this is personalized, targeted phishing = spear phishing. Generic phishing doesn't include personal details. (2) Malware-laden file/link: A link that installs malware when clicked = file-based or URL-based malware delivery. (3) Flat network / no segmentation: If malware could spread to ALL systems, there were no network segments to contain it. Proper segmentation would have limited spread. (4) APT dwell time: 6 months undetected is characteristic of an Advanced Persistent Threat — long-term, low-and-slow access. This is why insider threat detection and SIEM/anomaly detection matter. (5) Missing logs / log tampering: No logs for critical systems during the attack = attacker covered tracks by deleting logs. This is a named Security+ indicator of malicious activity.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key B is the only consistent mapping, but the five-part matching format is unlike the real exam and the other options are obviously absurd.

questions.question: An employee posts negative comments about their employer on social media after being passed over for promotion, then shares confidential client data with a competitor. What threat actor type is this?
questions.justification: Three insider threat types: (1) Malicious = deliberately harms the organization, motivated by revenge, financial gain, or ideology. (2) Negligent = accidental harm through poor practices (leaving laptop unlocked, clicking phishing links). (3) Compromised = external attacker has stolen their credentials. This scenario is clearly malicious — intentional data sharing with a competitor motivated by revenge. The social media posts reveal the revenge motivation. Key indicator: deliberate, intentional action with clear motive.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Malicious insider (disgruntled employee)) is correct for SY0-701 2.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A developer fails to validate the length of user-supplied input for a username field. An attacker enters a specially crafted username that overwrites adjacent memory and executes arbitrary code. What vulnerability type is this?
questions.justification: Buffer overflow occurs when input exceeds the allocated memory buffer, overwriting adjacent memory. Attackers craft input to overwrite the return address on the stack and redirect execution to their shellcode. Root cause: no input length validation. Mitigations: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), DEP/NX (Data Execution Prevention), stack canaries, input validation. SQL injection attacks databases, not memory. Race conditions involve timing issues. Format string attacks exploit printf-style format specifiers.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Buffer overflow) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A web application displays search results by inserting user input directly into SQL queries without sanitization. An attacker enters: ' OR '1'='1 — and retrieves all records in the database. What is this attack?
questions.justification: SQL injection inserts malicious SQL code into input fields that are incorporated into database queries. The ' OR '1'='1 input breaks the query logic so it returns ALL records (1=1 is always true). Prevention: parameterized queries/prepared statements, input validation, least privilege database accounts, stored procedures. XSS injects JavaScript into web pages. Command injection runs OS commands. LDAP injection attacks directory queries. The SQL payload ' OR '1'='1 is the classic SQLi signature.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (SQL Injection (SQLi)) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A researcher discovers a previously unknown vulnerability in a widely used SSL library. No patch exists yet. Security teams are unable to fully protect against exploitation. What is this type of vulnerability called?
questions.justification: Zero-day = a vulnerability unknown to the vendor/public, with no patch available. "Zero days" of warning for defenders. Exploits targeting zero-days are zero-day exploits. Mitigations when you can't patch: network segmentation, WAF rules, IPS signatures, monitoring, and anomaly detection. Example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) — days between public disclosure and exploitation were zero. Compare: Legacy vulnerabilities have known patches but unpatched systems. Supply chain = compromised vendor software/hardware.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Zero-day vulnerability) is correct for SY0-701 2.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A system administrator notices the web server is making outbound connections to an IP address in Eastern Europe on port 443, and sending small but regular packets at 3 AM every day. What is the MOST likely explanation?
questions.justification: C2 (Command and Control) beaconing is malware checking in with its controller. Classic indicators: regular intervals (beaconing), unusual outbound connections, suspicious destination IPs/countries, small packet sizes (just checking for commands), use of common ports like 443 to blend with HTTPS traffic. The 3 AM timing is off-hours to avoid detection. The pattern — regular, small, same destination — is a strong C2 indicator. Certificate renewals don't beacon to foreign IPs; updates don't go to random Eastern European addresses.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (C2 (Command and Control) beaconing) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A user reports that their files have been renamed with ".locked" extensions and they see a message demanding cryptocurrency payment for decryption. What type of malware is this?
questions.justification: Ransomware encrypts victim files and demands payment (usually cryptocurrency) for the decryption key. Indicators: encrypted files with unusual extensions (.locked, .crypt, .encrypted), ransom note, files inaccessible. Examples: WannaCry, NotPetya, REvil, LockBit. Prevention: offline backups (3-2-1 rule), email filtering, patching, network segmentation. Rootkit = hides itself and other malware from the OS. Trojan = disguises as legitimate software. Logic bomb = triggers on specific conditions (date, action).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Ransomware) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Security tools detect that a process is reading all files on a drive and sending them to an external FTP server. The process has a name matching a legitimate Windows system utility. What type of malware behavior is MOST consistent with this?

options.text: Data exfiltration by a Trojan masquerading as a system process

questions.justification: This describes two behaviors: (1) Process masquerading — naming malware after legitimate utilities (svchost.exe, lsass.exe, etc.) to avoid detection. (2) Data exfiltration — reading files and sending to external servers. Trojans disguise themselves as legitimate software. Data exfiltration is a key indicator of compromise (IOC). FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) and EDR tools detect unusual process behaviors. UEBA flags processes doing unusual amounts of file reads. Ransomware would encrypt files, not exfiltrate them; DDoS would send network traffic outward without file reading.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Data exfiltration by a Trojan masquerading as a system process) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An antivirus tool detects suspicious behavior based on the actions a program takes (reading registry keys, modifying startup entries, making network connections), rather than matching a known signature. What detection method is this?
questions.justification: Behavior-based (anomaly) detection monitors WHAT a program does, not what it looks like. Effective against zero-days and polymorphic malware that evades signatures. Signature-based = matches hash or byte patterns against known malware database. Heuristic = static analysis of code structure looking for suspicious patterns before execution. Behavior-based = dynamic analysis of runtime actions. Reputation-based = checks file/URL reputation against threat intel feeds. Modern EDR uses all methods but behavior-based is most effective against novel threats.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key C (behavior-based detection) matches runtime-action monitoring; heuristic (B) is static code analysis, so C is the better fit.

questions.question: An organization discovers that an attacker has been on their network for 3 months using stolen credentials. Which mitigation technique would have MOST effectively limited the blast radius of this compromise?

options.text: Network segmentation and least privilege access

questions.justification: When credentials are stolen, the attacker has legitimate access — AV won't catch them. Patching doesn't help. The best mitigation is limiting what those credentials CAN access: network segmentation (VLANs limit lateral movement between segments) + least privilege (stolen credentials only reach minimum necessary resources). "Blast radius" = scope of damage from a breach. Zero trust + micro-segmentation + least privilege = attackers can't easily move laterally even with valid credentials. This is the core defense against APT-style attacks.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Network segmentation and least privilege access) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company deploys software that intercepts and analyzes all outbound email and web traffic, blocking employees from sending files containing credit card numbers or Social Security numbers to external destinations. What security tool is this?
questions.justification: DLP inspects content in motion, at rest, and in use, and enforces policies to prevent sensitive data from leaving the organization. It understands DATA context — credit card patterns (Luhn algorithm), SSN patterns, health records — not just IP addresses or ports. Firewalls work at network layer (ports/IPs), not content. IDS detects attacks but doesn't inspect email content for PII. SIEM aggregates logs. DLP = content-aware data protection = PCI DSS and HIPAA compliance tool.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (DLP (Data Loss Prevention)) is correct for SY0-701 4.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker inserts a modified USB drive into a target's car. The USB is labeled "Employee Salary Data Q3." An employee finds it in the parking lot and plugs it into their work laptop. What technique is this?
questions.justification: Baiting exploits curiosity or greed — leaving infected USB drives in public areas where employees will find and insert them. The enticing label ("Salary Data") increases the likelihood of plugging it in. This technique was used in real attacks (Stuxnet was spread partially via USB drives). Defense: disable USB autorun/autoplay, block unknown USB devices via endpoint controls, security awareness training. This is a physical/social engineering vector combining removable media + human curiosity.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key A (baiting via removable media) is correct; the stem's 'inserts a USB drive into a target's car' vs 'found in the parking lot' wording is slightly confusing.

questions.question: An organization's web application uses a third-party analytics library loaded from an external CDN. The CDN is compromised and the library is modified to steal user credentials. What vulnerability category does this represent?
questions.justification: Supply chain attacks target the software/hardware supply chain — compromising a dependency (library, CDN, update mechanism) that gets distributed to many victims. The application itself is not directly attacked; the attack travels through trusted third-party code. Famous examples: SolarWinds Orion (compromised update mechanism), NotPetya (spread through Ukrainian accounting software), and npm/PyPI package poisoning. Defenses: Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes for CDN content, SBOM (Software Bill of Materials), vendor risk assessments.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Supply chain vulnerability) is correct for SY0-701 2.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security analyst observes that a Windows host is running a legitimate-looking process named "svch0st.exe" (with a zero, not the letter O). What type of malware technique does this represent?

options.text: Process masquerading / Living off the land

questions.justification: Process masquerading names malware after legitimate Windows processes (svchost.exe, lsass.exe, explorer.exe) with subtle modifications (zero for O, double letters). This helps malware blend in with normal process lists. Defense: check process path (real svchost.exe runs from C:\Windows\System32, not Desktop), verify digital signature, use process monitoring tools like Process Monitor. "Living off the land" specifically uses legitimate OS tools (PowerShell, WMI, certutil) for malicious purposes to avoid AV detection.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key B is the intended answer (process masquerading), but the option bundles 'Living off the land', which does not describe a renamed binary; the option label should be fixed.

questions.question: Which mitigation technique involves preventing executables from running in directories where users can write files (like %TEMP% or %AppData%)?
questions.justification: Application allowlisting (whitelisting) only permits approved executables to run. AppLocker and Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) can block execution from user-writable directories — a powerful anti-malware technique since most malware drops into temp directories. This stops fileless malware delivery and prevents users from accidentally running malicious executables. Allowlisting is more secure but harder to manage than blocklisting (blacklisting). This directly mitigates many phishing and drive-by attack chains.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Application allowlisting / Execution prevention) is correct for SY0-701 2.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An attacker sends a text message appearing to be from a bank saying "Suspicious login detected. Click here to verify your account" with a link to a fake bank website. What attack type is this?
questions.justification: Smishing = SMS/text-message phishing. The vector is the text message. Vishing = voice call. Phishing/spear phishing = email. Pharming = DNS manipulation. Quick reference: Phishing (email) → Spear phishing (targeted email) → Whaling (targeted C-suite email) → Smishing (SMS) → Vishing (voice). The key distinguisher is the DELIVERY VECTOR. Any question with "text message" or "SMS" = smishing. Any question with "phone call" = vishing.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Smishing) is correct for SY0-701 2.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A log shows a user account from accounting successfully authenticated to 47 different servers in 8 minutes — far beyond normal behavior. What type of attack indicator is this MOST consistent with?
questions.justification: Lateral movement = an attacker moving through the network using compromised credentials to reach additional systems. Indicators: authentication to many systems in short time, unusual service account access patterns, use of admin tools (PsExec, WMI, RDP) across multiple hosts. An accounting user connecting to 47 servers in 8 minutes is anomalous — legitimate users don't do this. UEBA and SIEM correlation rules are designed to detect exactly this pattern. This is often the post-exploitation phase after initial credential theft.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Lateral movement after credential compromise) is correct for SY0-701 2.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company implements endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools on all workstations. EDR is PRIMARILY designed to:

options.text: Prevent all malware from executing using signature databases
Monitor, detect, investigate, and respond to threats on endpoints in real time
Encrypt endpoint storage to prevent data theft

questions.justification: EDR goes beyond traditional AV. questions.question: A malware sample changes its own code and signature every time it replicates to evade signature-based detection. What type of malware is this?

questions.question: Which type of security control is an IDS an example of?

questions.question: Health records protected under HIPAA are classified as which type of data?

questions.question: Data that is actively being processed in memory by an application is in which state?
questions.justification: Data in Use refers to data actively being processed, accessed, or modified by applications or users — residing in memory (RAM) or being processed by a CPU. questions.question: Which data security method replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive equivalent that CANNOT be reverse-engineered to reveal the original data?
questions.justification: Tokenization replaces sensitive data (like a credit card number) with a non-sensitive token. The token can be used for processing but cannot be reverse-engineered to reveal the original. Masking hides portions of real data (shows last 4 digits). Hashing is one-way but produces a hash of the original — used for integrity, not substitution. Obfuscation makes data harder to understand.

questions.question: An organization must ensure data stored in Germany complies with EU laws. This requirement relates to which concept?

questions.question: Which backup type copies ONLY data that has changed since the last backup of ANY type (full or incremental)?

questions.question: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is BEST defined as:

The maximum time a system can be down before it must be restored
The cost of restoring systems after a failure event

questions.justification: RTO = how long the system can be DOWN (downtime tolerance). RPO = how much DATA can be lost (data loss tolerance). Memory trick: RTO = Time to Operate again. A discussion-based simulation to evaluate disaster response procedures without interrupting systems

questions.question: A network architect places web servers in a zone accessible from the internet, separate from internal database servers. What network architecture concept is being implemented?

questions.question: Which firewall type examines the full content of network packets including the application-layer payload and can detect threats hidden within allowed protocols like HTTP or DNS?

questions.question: A security device is positioned inline on the network and can automatically DROP malicious traffic when an attack signature is detected — not just alert. What is this device?

questions.question: What does "infrastructure as code" (IaC) security mean in a cloud context?

questions.question: An organization needs to protect sensitive data stored in a database so that even if the storage media is stolen, the data cannot be read without the correct key. What control addresses this?
questions.justification: Encryption at rest protects stored data — if storage media is physically stolen, the data is unreadable without the decryption key. Three data states: at rest (stored), in transit (moving over network — TLS/HTTPS), in use (being processed — memory encryption like AMD SEV). Data masking = replaces data with realistic but fake data (dev/test environments). Tokenization = replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive token (PCI DSS for credit cards). questions.question: A company has a critical database server. They implement a secondary server that continuously receives real-time copies of all transactions. If the primary fails, the secondary takes over automatically within seconds. What HA concept is this?
questions.justification: Active-passive HA: primary (active) handles all traffic; secondary (passive) receives real-time data sync and sits ready. Automatic failover within seconds — near-zero downtime. This is different from: Load balancing (active-active — both servers share traffic simultaneously). Warm standby = partially provisioned, manual or slow failover. Cold site = empty facility, must provision from scratch (hours/days). The combination of "real-time copies" + "automatic failover" + "seconds" = active-passive HA clustering (near-zero RTO).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (High availability clustering / Active-passive failover) is correct for SY0-701 3.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: After a disaster destroys the primary data center, the organization needs to resume operations at an alternate site within 4 hours. The alternate site has pre-configured servers and network equipment but no live data. What type of DR site is this?
questions.justification: DR site comparison: Hot site = fully operational mirror (real-time data sync, immediate failover, minutes RTO). Warm site = pre-configured hardware, no live data — need to restore from backup before operations resume (hours RTO). Cold site = empty space/power/cooling, must bring in hardware (days/weeks RTO). The scenario: "pre-configured servers/network" (not cold) + "no live data" (not hot) + 4-hour RTO = warm site. Warm sites balance cost (cheaper than hot) with reasonable recovery time.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Warm site) is correct for SY0-701 3.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company wants to inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic for malware without the user receiving certificate errors. Which technique allows this?

options.text: TLS/SSL inspection (interception) with trusted enterprise CA

questions.justification: SSL inspection (TLS interception) performs a man-in-the-middle by the proxy: the proxy terminates the client's TLS session, inspects the plaintext, re-encrypts and forwards. To avoid certificate errors, the enterprise deploys its own CA certificate as trusted on all managed endpoints. The proxy presents dynamically generated certificates signed by this CA. Privacy concern: employees should be notified. Legal consideration: may require acceptable use policy. Enables inspection of C2 traffic hiding in HTTPS and malware in encrypted downloads.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (TLS/SSL inspection (interception) with trusted enterprise CA) is correct for SY0-701 3.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company sets up a decoy server on their network that appears to be a real production server but contains no legitimate data. Its purpose is to detect and study attacker behavior. What is this?
questions.justification: Honeypot = a single decoy system designed to attract attackers and monitor their behavior. Any access to the honeypot is inherently suspicious (no legitimate users should access it). Honeynet = multiple honeypots forming a network — simulates a whole environment. Sandbox = isolated environment for safely executing and analyzing potentially malicious files. Canary token = a digital tripwire (fake document, link, credential) that alerts when accessed. Honeypots/honeynets help: early detection, attacker TTP (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures) research, slow down attackers.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (Honeypot) is correct for SY0-701 1.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A backup strategy creates a full backup every Sunday, a differential backup every other day. If the system fails Thursday, which backups must be restored?

options.text: Sunday full + Monday diff + Tuesday diff + Wednesday diff

questions.justification: Key difference: Differential backup = ALL changes since the last FULL backup. Each day's diff grows larger but contains everything. Restore = 2 steps: full + latest diff. Incremental backup = ONLY changes since last backup (any type). Restore = full + every incremental in order. With differential: Thursday restore = Sunday full + Wednesday diff (which contains ALL changes since Sunday, including Mon/Tue). With incremental: Thursday restore = Sunday + Monday + Tuesday + Wednesday (4 tapes). Differential: faster restore, larger backups. Incremental: slower restore, smaller backups.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Sunday full + Wednesday differential only) is correct for SY0-701 3.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which cloud computing characteristic allows resources (compute, storage, bandwidth) to automatically scale up during peak demand and scale down during off-peak times?
questions.justification: NIST defines 5 essential cloud characteristics: (1) On-demand self-service, (2) Broad network access, (3) Resource pooling, (4) Rapid elasticity, (5) Measured service. Rapid elasticity = capabilities can be provisioned and released on demand, quickly scaling with demand. Example: auto-scaling groups that add servers during Black Friday traffic spikes. Resource pooling = provider serves multiple customers from shared resources. Measured service = pay for what you use (metered). Broad network access = accessible via any device/network.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Rapid elasticity) is correct for SY0-701 3.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company wants to prevent sensitive data from traversing outside of specific VLANs without passing through a security inspection point. Which architectural approach achieves this?

options.text: East-west traffic inspection via micro-segmentation and internal firewalls

questions.justification: Traditional security focused on north-south traffic (in/out of the perimeter). Modern attacks move LATERALLY — east-west traffic (server to server within the network). Micro-segmentation creates fine-grained security zones with policies between them. Internal firewalls or software-defined security force all inter-VLAN traffic through inspection. Zero-trust architecture requires this. Prevents an attacker who compromises one segment from freely moving to others. NSX, Cisco ACI, and cloud security groups implement micro-segmentation. Port security controls which devices connect to switch ports, not traffic between VLANs.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (East-west traffic inspection via micro-segmentation and internal firewalls) is correct for SY0-701 3.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security analyst needs to securely delete files from a solid-state drive (SSD) that will be decommissioned. Which method is MOST effective for SSDs?

options.text: Standard delete and empty recycle bin
Cryptographic erasure (encrypting then discarding keys) or physical destruction

questions.justification: SSDs use wear leveling — data is written to different cells each time, so overwrite methods (DoD 7-pass) may not reach all copies. For SSDs: (1) Cryptographic erasure = if drive was encrypted, delete the key (data becomes permanently unreadable). (2) Physical destruction = shredding. (3) Secure Erase command (ATA Secure Erase) supported by some SSDs. Traditional overwrite methods designed for HDDs are unreliable on SSDs due to wear leveling and overprovisioning. NIST SP 800-88 provides guidance on media sanitization by storage type.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Cryptographic erasure (encrypting then discarding keys) or physical destruction) is correct for SY0-701 4.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which solution provides centralized visibility and control over cloud applications — including unsanctioned apps — and enforces security policies between users and cloud services?
questions.justification: CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) sits between users and cloud services, providing: (1) Visibility — what cloud apps are being used (shadow IT discovery). (2) Data security — DLP for cloud apps. (3) Threat protection — malware scanning. (4) Compliance — enforce policies. CASB can be proxy-based (inline) or API-based (direct integration). Examples: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, Netskope, Zscaler. WAF protects web applications. SIEM correlates logs. VPN encrypts tunnels. CASB = cloud governance + shadow IT + data protection in the cloud.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker)) is correct for SY0-701 3.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company follows the 3-2-1 backup rule. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes this rule?

options.text: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite
3 backups per day, 2 full backups per week, 1 offsite rotation per month
3 data centers, 2 are active, 1 is cold standby

questions.justification: 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 = three total copies of your data (1 primary + 2 backups). 2 = stored on two different media types (e.g., local disk + tape, or local disk + cloud). 1 = at least one copy stored offsite (protects against site disasters — fire, flood, theft). Why different media? Protects against media-specific failures. Why offsite? Protects against site-wide disasters. Extended: 3-2-1-1-0 adds: 1 copy immutable (offline/air-gapped, ransomware-proof) + 0 backup errors (test restores). Most important exam rule for backup strategy.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite) is correct for SY0-701 3.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security team deploys a system that monitors the behavior of users and entities across the environment, using machine learning to establish baselines and alert on anomalous activity. What type of system is this?
questions.justification: UEBA = User and Entity Behavior Analytics. Uses ML/AI to build behavioral baselines for users and devices, then flags deviations. Detects: impossible travel, unusual data access volumes, off-hours logins, lateral movement, privilege abuse. SIEM collects and correlates logs from many sources — often integrates UEBA. IPS blocks signature-based network attacks. DLP prevents data exfiltration. UEBA specifically focuses on behavioral anomalies vs. signatures — effective against insider threats and APTs that don't trigger traditional signatures.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics)) is correct for SY0-701 4.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A smart building controller manages HVAC and lighting systems and connects to the corporate network for management. What security risk does this IoT device PRIMARILY introduce?

options.text: Expanded attack surface — a compromised IoT device can pivot to the corporate network

questions.justification: IoT devices connected to corporate networks create attack surfaces. They often have: default credentials, unpatched firmware, no endpoint protection, no encryption. A compromised IoT device can be used as a pivot point to attack higher-value systems. Famous real example: Target 2013 breach — attackers entered via an HVAC vendor's credentials and pivoted to the payment network. Mitigations: IoT in separate VLAN, firmware updates, change default credentials, network monitoring, disable unnecessary services. The Target breach made "HVAC as attack vector" a classic exam reference.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Expanded attack surface — a compromised IoT device can pivot to the corporate ne) is correct for SY0-701 3.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company classifies its data into four categories: Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted. Restricted data requires encryption at rest and in transit, MFA, and logging of all access. What is this classification activity part of?
questions.justification: Data classification assigns sensitivity levels to data and defines handling requirements for each level. This is foundational to data governance — you can't protect data you haven't categorized. Classification drives encryption requirements, access controls, retention policies, and disposal procedures. Government: Top Secret/Secret/Confidential/Unclassified. Private sector: Restricted/Confidential/Internal/Public. The Data Owner defines classification; the Data Custodian implements controls; users are responsible for following policy. Classification = foundation of all other data protection measures.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Data governance and classification policy) is correct for SY0-701 3.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's on-premises application authenticates users against Active Directory, while its cloud applications authenticate through Azure AD. What technology allows users to use a single set of credentials across both environments?
questions.justification: Identity federation = linking identity systems across different domains/organizations so users can use one identity across multiple systems. SSO (Single Sign-On) = one login grants access to multiple applications. Technologies: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) for web apps, OAuth 2.0 for authorization, OpenID Connect for authentication. Azure AD Connect federates on-premises AD with cloud Azure AD. Benefits: fewer passwords, better user experience, centralized access control. RADIUS = network access authentication. LDAP = directory query protocol. Kerberos = enterprise ticket-based auth (on-premises only).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Identity federation / SSO) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which embedded security chip on a laptop motherboard stores encryption keys, digital certificates, and can attest to the integrity of the boot process?
questions.justification: TPM is a hardware chip on the motherboard that: stores cryptographic keys (BitLocker uses TPM for full disk encryption keys), provides a hardware root of trust, enables measured boot (hashes each boot component to detect tampering), supports remote attestation (proves to a remote server that the system is in a trusted state). BitLocker requires TPM 2.0 (Windows 11 requirement). HSM = enterprise-grade, separate device for high-security key management. Secure Enclave = Apple's equivalent in iPhone/Mac processors. Smart card = portable token for authentication.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer A (TPM (Trusted Platform Module)) is correct for SY0-701 1.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization's BCP states that the order fulfillment system must never experience more than 2 hours of downtime. What BIA metric defines this requirement?
questions.justification: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = maximum acceptable downtime before business impact becomes unacceptable. "Must not experience more than 2 hours of downtime" = RTO of 2 hours. RPO = max acceptable data loss (how old can backups be?). MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) = average time to repair a COMPONENT (reactive/operational metric). MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) = average time between failures (reliability metric). RTO and RPO are forward-looking planning metrics set during BIA. MTTR and MTBF are historical operational metrics used to evaluate system reliability.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (RTO) is correct for SY0-701 5.2; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company implements NAC (Network Access Control). What is the PRIMARY function of NAC?

options.text: Block external threats at the firewall
Verify device compliance (patches, AV, configuration) before allowing network access

questions.justification: NAC (Network Access Control) evaluates connecting devices against security policies before granting network access. Checks: Is the OS patched? Is AV installed and updated? Is the firewall enabled? Is disk encryption on? Non-compliant devices are quarantined to a remediation VLAN until they meet requirements. Example: 802.1X uses NAC for port-based access control. Cisco ISE is a popular NAC solution. NAC enforces "health checks" — you must be healthy to join the network. Prevents BYOD devices with outdated software from being attack vectors on the corporate network.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer D (Verify device compliance (patches, AV, configuration) before allowing network ac) is correct for SY0-701 4.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security administrator is deploying Ansible playbooks across 500 workstations to enforce password complexity, disable USB storage, and enable host-based firewalls. Which phase of secure baseline management does this represent?
questions.justification: The three phases of secure baseline management are Establish (define the baseline), Deploy (push it to systems), and Maintain (audit and keep it current). Using Ansible to push configurations across 500 workstations is the Deploy phase — automated tooling distributing the already-defined baseline. Establish (A) would be the activity of writing the playbook and defining the security requirements. Maintain (C) involves ongoing audits after deployment to verify the baseline persists. Audit (D) is part of Maintain, not its own separate phase in this framework.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Deploy) is correct for SY0-701 4.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization discovers that several smart HVAC controllers on their network still use the manufacturer's default username and password. What is the MOST critical first hardening step?

options.text: Encrypt all traffic between HVAC controllers and the management server
Place the HVAC controllers in a separate network segment

questions.justification: IoT and embedded device security always starts with changing default credentials — this is the #1 IoT hardening step on the exam. Default passwords are publicly documented by manufacturers and are the first thing attackers try. While all other options (encryption, firmware updates, segmentation) are also valid hardening steps, the MOST CRITICAL and immediate first action is always changing default passwords. Default credentials make the device trivially compromisable in seconds — no sophistication required.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Change the default passwords immediately) is correct for SY0-701 4.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company allows employees to use their personal iPhones to access corporate email. The security team installs MDM software that can remotely wipe devices. Which mobile deployment model is this?
questions.justification: BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) — employees bring personal devices to work and access corporate resources. The company manages the corporate data/apps via MDM but does not own the device. COPE (A) = company buys the device and allows personal use; here the employee owns the iPhone. CYOD (B) = employee picks from a company-approved device list; here the employee chose their own device with no company approval required. MDM (D) is the management technology used within a deployment model, not the deployment model itself.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (BYOD) is correct for SY0-701 4.1; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A penetration tester runs Burp Suite against a web application and discovers that user input in a search field is executed directly in the database. What vulnerability was identified, and what is the correct input validation best practice to prevent it?

options.text: XSS; use blacklisting to block known-bad input
SQL injection; use whitelisting to accept only known-good input
Buffer overflow; use static code analysis
SQL injection; use blacklisting to block SQL keywords

questions.justification: User input executed directly in a database is SQL injection. The correct prevention is whitelisting — accepting only known-good input formats (numbers only, alphanumeric, specific character sets), not blacklisting. Blacklisting (blocking known-bad like "DROP TABLE" or "SELECT *") is easily bypassed with encoding tricks, case variations, or new SQL syntax. Whitelisting is fundamentally stronger because everything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Option D describes SQL injection correctly but specifies the wrong control. XSS (A) is JavaScript injection into web pages, not database queries. Buffer overflow (C) is a memory management issue, not user input to a database.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key B (SQL injection; allow-list validation) is the best option offered; parameterized queries would be the primary control, but among these choices B is correct and D uses the weaker deny-list.

questions.question: A vulnerability scanner reports a CVE with a Base Score of 9.8, Temporal Score of 8.1 (patch available), and Environmental Score of 6.2 (affected system is isolated with no internet access). Which score should the security team use to prioritize remediation?

options.text: Base Score 9.8 — always use base score for prioritization
Temporal Score 8.1 — the patch availability reduces urgency
Environmental Score 6.2 — it reflects the actual risk in their specific context

questions.justification: The Environmental Score is the most meaningful for prioritization because it accounts for the organization's specific context — in this case, the system is isolated with no internet access, which significantly reduces exploitability. The Base Score (A) reflects intrinsic characteristics without considering your environment. The Temporal Score (B) adjusts for current exploit availability but still ignores your specific environment. CVSS was designed so that environmental scoring gives the most actionable risk rating for your organization. A critical CVE on an isolated system that handles non-sensitive data is much lower priority than a medium CVE on an internet-facing payment system.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Environmental Score 6.2 — it reflects the actual risk in their specific context) is correct for SY0-701 4.3; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security team's vulnerability scanner flags a library as "End of Life with known critical CVE" on a web server. Upon investigation, the library is not loaded by any active code path. This is BEST described as:

options.text: False negative — the scanner missed a real vulnerability
True positive — the library is present and should be removed
False positive — the scanner flagged a non-exploitable condition
Exception — the risk should be accepted and documented

questions.justification: This is a true positive — the library IS present, IS end-of-life, and DOES have a critical CVE. The scanner correctly identified a real condition. The fact that no active code path currently loads it does not make it a false positive — the library still exists on the system and could be called in the future, or exploited directly if an attacker gains access to the filesystem. The correct action is to remove the library (or update it). A false positive (C) would mean the vulnerability doesn't actually exist. A false negative (A) would mean the scanner missed an existing vulnerability. An exception (D) requires formal risk acceptance documentation — even then, the finding is still real, so B remains the most accurate description of what the scanner found.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Key B is defensible: the EOL library with a critical CVE is actually present, so the finding is real (true positive) even if not currently loaded; some instructors might argue false positive, lowering realism.

questions.question: Which tool would BEST provide a visual real-time overview of network traffic volume, top talkers, and sudden traffic spikes that could indicate a DDoS attack?
questions.justification: NetFlow is specifically designed to collect and analyze network traffic flow data — volume, direction, top talkers, protocol breakdown. It's ideal for detecting DDoS (sudden traffic spikes from many sources) and data exfiltration (large outbound transfers). Nessus (A) is a vulnerability scanner — it scans for weaknesses, not traffic patterns. SIEM (C) aggregates logs and correlates events — it could receive NetFlow data as an input, but the question asks for the tool providing that real-time traffic visualization. DLP (D) prevents sensitive data from leaving — not traffic volume analysis. NetFlow is the specific technology for network traffic analytics and pattern detection.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (NetFlow analyzer (e.g., SolarWinds)) is correct for SY0-701 4.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: An organization wants to ensure that only Windows workstations with up-to-date antivirus signatures and full-disk encryption enabled can connect to the corporate network. Which technology enforces this?
questions.justification: Network Access Control (NAC) checks device posture (health) before allowing network access. It enforces conditions like: AV signatures must be current, disk encryption must be enabled, OS must have required patches. Devices that fail posture checks are quarantined or denied access. EDR (A) monitors and responds to threats on already-connected endpoints — it doesn't control whether a device can join the network. DLP (B) prevents data from leaving the network — not a connection control mechanism. FIM (D) monitors file and config changes — not network admission. The keyword "connect to the corporate network" + "condition-based" = NAC.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (NAC) is correct for SY0-701 4.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's email logs show that their domain is being used to send phishing emails from IP addresses not owned by the company. Which email authentication record specifies which IP addresses are authorized to send email for the domain?
questions.justification: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a DNS TXT record that lists the authorized IP addresses and mail servers allowed to send email on behalf of the domain. When a receiving mail server gets an email, it checks the sending IP against the domain's SPF record — if the IP isn't listed, the email fails SPF. This directly addresses the scenario: unauthorized IPs sending email for your domain. DKIM (A) validates message integrity with a cryptographic signature — it doesn't list authorized IPs. DMARC (B) is the policy layer that tells receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail — it depends on SPF and DKIM being configured first. SMTP relay (D) is a mail server configuration term, not an authentication standard.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (SPF) is correct for SY0-701 4.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Analysts receive 800+ alerts per day from the SIEM, and real threats are being missed because analysts are overwhelmed. Which action BEST addresses this problem?

options.text: Implement alert tuning to reduce false positives

questions.justification: Alert tuning (adjusting detection thresholds and correlation rules to reduce false positives) directly addresses alert fatigue — the condition where too many low-quality alerts cause analysts to miss real threats. By refining what triggers alerts, the signal-to-noise ratio improves without disabling monitoring entirely. Adding SIEM instances (A) adds capacity but doesn't fix alert quality — you'd still get 800+ alerts per day. Disabling alert categories (C) is dangerous — you might disable detection of a real attack vector. Adding analysts (D) treats the symptom but not the cause — the better answer is to fix the alert quality first. Alert tuning is the correct operational response to alert fatigue.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Implement alert tuning to reduce false positives) is correct for SY0-701 4.4; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: Which access control model is being used when a Linux administrator configures SELinux security contexts to prevent a compromised Apache web server process from accessing /etc/passwd even if it's running as root?
questions.justification: SELinux enforces Mandatory Access Control — the system (kernel) enforces security policy that users and processes cannot override, even root. MAC uses labels/contexts to determine access. The Apache process has a specific SELinux context that doesn't include permission to read /etc/passwd, regardless of file owner permissions or the process running as root. This is MAC's defining characteristic: the OS enforces policy that overrides user/process discretion. DAC (A) would be standard Linux permissions where root CAN access anything. RBAC (B) assigns permissions based on job roles, not OS-level process contexts. ABAC (D) uses attribute-based policies — more complex and not how SELinux primarily operates.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (MAC — Mandatory Access Control) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A financial institution uses a system where an analyst must request admin rights for a 2-hour maintenance window. The rights are granted automatically and revoked at the end of the window without any additional action. This is an example of:
questions.justification: Just-in-Time (JIT) permissions grant temporary elevated access for a defined window and automatically revoke it when the window expires. Key indicators: time-limited, auto-revoked, requested on-demand. This is JIT. Ephemeral credentials (A) are auto-generated temporary credentials (like AWS short-lived tokens) — they are temporary like JIT, but the distinguishing factor is they're typically generated per-session for automated systems, not human-requested maintenance windows. Password vaulting (B) is securely storing privileged credentials in an encrypted vault — not the same as time-limiting access. RBAC (D) is role-based permissions — it doesn't inherently involve time limits or auto-revocation.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Just-in-Time permissions) is correct for SY0-701 4.6; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: During an incident, a security analyst isolates a compromised workstation from the network while preserving its state for investigation. What IR phase does this action belong to, and what is the specific action called?
questions.justification: Containment is the IR phase focused on stopping the spread of an incident — limiting blast radius without destroying evidence. Quarantine is the specific action of isolating a system from the network (removing its ability to communicate) while keeping it powered on for forensic analysis. Key: "preserving its state" means this is not eradication (which removes the threat) and not recovery (which restores normal operations). Containment = stop the bleeding. Quarantine = the specific isolation mechanism. Eradication (A) comes after containment — it removes the malware/threat from the system. Detection (C) is earlier in the cycle — identifying that an incident occurred. Recovery (D) is after eradication — restoring systems to normal operation.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (Containment phase; quarantine) is correct for SY0-701 4.8; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A security team conducts a meeting where they walk through a hypothetical ransomware attack scenario, discussing what each team member would do at each stage. No systems are touched. What type of exercise is this?
questions.justification: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based exercise where participants talk through a hypothetical scenario without touching any actual systems. Low cost, low disruption, reveals gaps in plans and communication. The key indicators here: meeting/discussion format, hypothetical scenario, no systems touched. A simulation (B) involves active, real-time exercises with actual system interactions — more complex and resource-intensive. Red team (A) exercises involve actual attacks against real systems by a team simulating adversaries. Penetration testing (D) is technical testing of specific systems for vulnerabilities, not an IR exercise. The "no systems touched" and "discussion" elements are the defining characteristics of a tabletop.
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer C (Tabletop exercise) is correct for SY0-701 4.8; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A forensics investigator creates a SHA-256 hash of a hard drive image immediately after acquisition. The same hash is verified at every step of the investigation. What does this protect?
questions.justification: Correct Answer: B. Hashing the forensic image right after acquisition and re-verifying the same SHA-256 value at every step proves the evidence has not changed, which preserves its integrity and admissibility. A is wrong because chain of custody is the documented record of who handled the evidence and when; hashing complements it but is not the same thing. C is wrong because hashing is a one-way integrity function and does not encrypt data or provide confidentiality. D is wrong because a legal hold is the directive to preserve potentially relevant data, not a technical integrity check.
questions.review_notes: SME review: incorrect_key - Source options are out of order (A, C, B, D) and the key 'C' points to 'Data confidentiality via encryption'; hashing an image at acquisition and re-verifying protects evidence integrity/preservation, which is option B.; AI-drafted explanation pending editor approval

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY difference between EDR and XDR?

options.text: EDR is more expensive than XDR
XDR integrates endpoint, network, and cloud data into one platform; EDR focuses only on endpoints
EDR uses AI; XDR uses signature-based detection
XDR replaces SIEM; EDR replaces antivirus

questions.justification: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) focuses on monitoring, detecting, and responding to threats specifically on endpoints (workstations, servers, mobile devices). XDR (Extended Detection and Response) extends that scope by integrating data from endpoints + network + cloud + email + identity systems into a unified platform. XDR provides broader visibility and can correlate an attack across multiple vectors simultaneously — an EDR alone might see suspicious endpoint behavior but miss the network traffic context that reveals the full attack chain. XDR doesn't replace SIEM (D) — they serve different functions. Cost (A) is not the defining difference. Both EDR and XDR use behavioral analytics and AI (C).
questions.review_notes: SME review: correct - Keyed answer B (XDR integrates endpoint, network, and cloud data into one platform; EDR focuses ) is correct for SY0-701 4.5; distractors are clearly wrong.

questions.question: A company's security policy requires that an employee's access rights be revoked automatically within minutes of their termination being processed in HR. Which automation use case addresses this?
questions.justification: Automatically enabling or disabling user access based on status changes (hired, terminated, role change) is the automation use case of enabling/disabling services and access. When HR processes a termination, this triggers an automated workflow that disables Active Directory accounts, revokes VPN certificates, removes email access, and deactivates badge credentials — all within minutes. Guard rails (A) are automated controls that prevent misconfiguration (e.g., can't create an unencrypted S3 bucket). Continuous integration (B) automates code testing in development pipelines. questions.question: A security engineer is configuring wireless security for a hospital network that handles ePHI. WPA2 is currently deployed. What should the engineer upgrade to, and why?

Stay on WPA2 — it meets all regulatory requirements for healthcare

questions.question: Which DMARC policy setting would cause emails that fail both SPF and DKIM checks to be silently dropped before reaching the recipient's inbox?

questions.question: A company must decommission 200 old laptops that contained confidential customer data. The IT team wants to reuse the hard drives in new equipment. Which is the MOST appropriate disposal method?

questions.question: Which authentication factor category does a YubiKey hardware security key belong to?

Simply accepting risk (A) without additional controls is not a responsible answer when compensating controls are available. questions.question: An organization implements a policy that users in the Finance department can only access financial records, and users in HR can only access HR records, with no cross-department access. This MOST closely describes which access control model?
questions.justification: Role-Based Access Control assigns permissions based on job role/function rather than individual identity. Finance role → Finance records access. HR role → HR records access. Access is managed at the role level — add a user to a role and they inherit all permissions for that role. This is RBAC's defining characteristic: role membership determines access. MAC (A) uses system-enforced labels and is more restrictive — users can't change their own access. DAC (C) lets resource owners grant access to whomever they choose — more flexible and user-controlled. questions.question: An ICS/SCADA system at a power plant cannot be taken offline for patching due to 24/7 operational requirements. The system runs on an outdated OS with known vulnerabilities. Which is the MOST appropriate security control?

These are compensating controls when patching is not feasible. Patching during a weekend (A) ignores the "24/7 operational requirements" — power plants don't get weekends off. questions.question: When collecting digital evidence from a compromised server, a forensic investigator captures RAM contents before powering off the system. Why is RAM captured BEFORE disk imaging?

RAM is more volatile — it's lost when the system powers off
RAM is more storage-efficient to capture
Disk data gets corrupted when RAM is captured after shutdown

questions.justification: The order of evidence collection follows the order of volatility — most volatile first. RAM (system memory) is completely lost the instant the system powers off. It contains running processes, network connections, decrypted data, encryption keys, malware that exists only in memory (fileless malware), user credentials, and command history. Once the power goes off, all of this is gone forever. Disk storage persists after power-off and can be captured later. This is why forensic investigators always capture RAM (memory dump) before disk imaging whenever possible. The other answers are incorrect: disk imaging speed (A) is irrelevant to the collection order. RAM capture doesn't affect disk integrity (D). RAM files can be very large — gigabytes — so C is also incorrect.

questions.question: A security policy requires that all servers be configured according to documented security baselines before production deployment. What is the PRIMARY benefit of using security baselines?

(4) Speed — new servers can be deployed from pre-hardened images. Baselines don't eliminate patching (B) — they define what to patch. They don't provide encryption or zero-day protection. questions.question: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) scores range from 0 to 10. Which score range indicates a CRITICAL severity vulnerability?
questions.justification: CVSS severity scale: None = 0.0, Low = 0.1-3.9, Medium = 4.0-6.9, High = 7.0-8.9, Critical = 9.0-10.0. A perfect 10.0 = network-exploitable, no authentication, no user interaction, maximum impact. Famous examples: Log4Shell (CVSS 10.0), Heartbleed (CVSS 7.5). CVSS considers: Attack Vector, Attack Complexity, Privileges Required, User Interaction, Scope, and three impact scores (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability). Critical vulns typically require immediate remediation (within 24-72 hours per most SLAs). High = within 30 days typically.

questions.question: A company implements a PAM (Privileged Access Management) solution. What is the PRIMARY purpose of PAM?

questions.justification: PAM specifically manages privileged accounts (admin, root, service accounts, shared credentials). Why critical: 80%+ of data breaches involve privileged credential abuse. PAM limits the "blast radius" of a privileged compromise. Examples: CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Thycotic. IAM = manages all user identities. PAM = the high-security subset managing privileged accounts specifically.

questions.question: An employee changes roles from HR to Finance. What access management process must be performed to ensure the principle of least privilege is maintained?

Delete the account and create a new one
De-provision HR access AND provision Finance access (role change process)
No action needed — access is managed automatically

If only new access is added (A), the employee retains unnecessary HR access they no longer need — violating least privilege. The correct process: revoke all HR permissions AND grant Finance permissions. This should be part of a formal offboarding/onboarding process triggered by HR system changes. Regular access reviews (recertification campaigns) catch accumulated access. User Lifecycle Management in IAM systems automates this through HRIS integration with provisioning systems.

questions.question: A forensic investigator discovers that file timestamps on a hard drive appear to have been modified to make recently created files appear older. What type of anti-forensic technique is this?

Attackers use it to hide when malicious files were placed on a system. Detection: MFT ($MFT) records on NTFS maintain multiple timestamps — some tools compare $STANDARD_INFORMATION (easily modified) vs. $FILE_NAME timestamps (harder to modify). Discrepancies indicate timestomping. Steganography = hiding data in files. Log deletion = removing event logs to hide activity. Data wiping = destroying evidence. Timestomping = manipulating WHEN evidence appears to have been created.

questions.question: Which technology intercepts DNS queries and compares requested domains against threat intelligence feeds, blocking connections to known malicious domains before they can establish?

questions.question: NetFlow data from a router shows a server exporting 50GB of data to an external IP at 2 AM. No scheduled transfers are known for this time. What type of monitoring data is NetFlow?
